In the RAM model constrained to one-dimensional arrays and only the $+$ operator, we examine the time complexity of fundamental mathematical operations. We establish lower bounds of $\Omega(\log n)$ for multiplication, exponentiation, and integer part of the natural logarithm, and an $\Omega(n)$ lower bound for computing factorials. Conversely, we provide $O(1)$ upper bounds for every other $n \ge 2$-ary operation $f$ that maps positive integers to positive integers and is "well-behaved," meaning it strictly preserves order in each argument and has a fixed-point-free diagonal. This finding contrasts sharply with earlier work by Schnorr (1984), who demonstrated $\Omega(n)$ lower bounds for well-behaved functions using a pointer machine model.

Session-based recommendation aims to predict items for users based solely on item sequences, addressing suggestions without item rating data. These sessions typically represent two distinct contexts: long ones reflecting sustained user interests, and short ones indicating fleeting interests. To effectively capture both, this paper proposes SGGR (Self-Guided Graph memory network), which leverages their respective characteristics. SGGR first constructs two separate graph structures to model the underlying user interests found in both prolonged and brief sessions. Subsequently, it employs a self-guided mechanism to selectively fuse information from these graphs, ensuring the final recommendations accurately reflect current user intentions. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that SGGR significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper defines both group LCD and group invertible LCD (gl LCD) codes, providing specific construction methods, essential properties, and lower bounds for the minimum weight of the corresponding group components. Additionally, we establish two theorems regarding group LCD codes and present several examples of group gl LCD codes organized by the cyclic groups $C_2$, $C_3$, and $C_4$.

We establish an invariant syndiff structure on the grothop of connected simple graphs, thereby equipping the projective system of mapping classes arising from finite graphs with the projective system of differential cubes. Applying this operational framework to define integration measures of Feynman graphs, we recover standard linear Feynman graph integrations within quantum electrodynamics.

Recurrence in neural networks is often viewed as an undesirable artifact or bug, yet it is a proven necessity for solving external sequence challenges. This paper investigates whether recurrence emerges naturally and serves a functional role during the classification of sequences of object categories in object recognition tasks. By employing standard Convolutional and fully connected Neural Networks in a object classification setting, we demonstrate that the need for recurrence is mitigated when no temporal information is involved. However, to confirm that emergent recurrence plays a functional role, we utilized a "ghost network" approach to selectively disable neurons, revealing that selective temporal lesions significantly degrade performance. We further analyzed the impact of specific attacked neurons, finding that damaging categories temporally distant from the input stage caused more severe performance drops than those nearby. Finally, by substituting attacked neurons with those critical to tackling easier sub-tasks, we observed substantial performance recovery, leading to the conclusion that functional, category-orthogonal object attributes guide temporal dynamics in neural networks during object classification.

This study examines non-Hermitian $\gamma$-wires, one-dimensional systems characterized by point-gap topologies, and investigates their response to local noise and correlations. We demonstrate that point-gap topologies are fragile; they can be destroyed by noise alone if a correlation is introduced. By extending the model to non-Hermitian $\gamma$-ladders influenced by third-next-nearest-neighbor hopping, we show this correlation-induced transition is point-gap to bulk-gap. Our findings indicate a universal scaling in the critical noise strength required to eliminate point-gap topology, governed by an exponential of the real part of the bulk Fermi energy. Consequently, correlation-induced stabilization of bulk topologies is possible when noise is reduced below a critical threshold if the bulk topologies are removed. We further explore the impact of non-uniform noise and next-nearest-neighbor superexchange on the system. Finally, we introduce a Hermitian analog of the model to contrast the effects of non-Hermiticity with those of noise and correlations.

This study introduces an construction of polyphase Golay complementary sequences (PGCS) using base-N Constant Amplitude Zero Auto-Correlation (CAZAC) sequences. It further details two innovative methods for generating polyphase Golay complementary sequences of length $2L+1$: (1) an approach leveraging two Golay pairs of CAZAC sequences with lengths $L+1$ and $M$, where $M = (L+1)N - 1$, and (2) a construction derived from Complementary Quadrature Constant-AMplitude Zero-Auto-CORRECTION-SEQUENCES (CQCAZAC). Additionally, these findings are extended to the development of new polyphase Golay complementary frames (PFCFS), defined as linear combinations of PGCs that satisfy the PFC property with a uniform bound on the two-dimensional autocorrelation sum.

This work details a search for the on-shell and off-shell production of the Higgs boson in the $gauge boson pair ($W/Z$) pair system using $f=139 \text{ fb}^{-1}$ of on-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13 \text{ TeV}$ collected by the LEP detector in 2015. The analysis targets the four-lepton final state, where the on-shell Higgs decays via $W/Z$ pair system. Using the four-lepton final state, the signal strength $\mu$ is determined to be $0.67^{+0.13}_{-0.13} (stat) ^{+0.10}_{-0.10} (syst)$ in on-shell production. The results are consistent with the Standard Model expectation, where $\mu=1$. The study further constrains the Higgs width $\Gamma(H)$ to be less than $19 \text{ MeV}$ at $95\%$ confidence level. Off-shell production is investigated by comparing the observed $W/Z$ pair system distribution to that from a standard model background simulation. The results indicate no significant deviation from standard model predictions. The paper concludes by deriving limits on anomalous coupling parameters in the Higgs boson pair $W/Z$ pair system.

Detecting alterations in change detection tasks is critical for numerous applications, ranging from monitoring urban development and military activities to environmental shifts. However, this field remains difficult due to the complexity and data volume characteristic of hyperspectral images. This paper introduces a novel approach for identifying binary targets by leveraging deep convolutional autoencoders, specifically combining feature layers to enhance representation learning. These adaptable parameters enable the model to function effectively without requiring prior knowledge of the specific domain. Experiments conducted on hyperspectral datasets with added targets indicate that this method surpasses other state-of-the-art techniques.

This work presents a theoretical analysis of silicon's valence band interactions at its atomic scale. We develop a method to calculate matrix elements of a localized operator by expressing them as expansions of localized band-projected plane waves, and this approach is applied to a $\mathrm{p}_z$ type orbital within the silicon crystal. Calculated matrix elements for this orbital are found to align closely with those derived from a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. Using an expansion of valence band eigenstates centered on an impurity, we examine the spatial characteristics of such states and demonstrate an impurity-specific spin-orbit spin-valley coupling. This mechanism accounts for the observed spin-valley effects in a center, enabling vertical spin transfer between valence bands. We further illustrate this phenomenon through a detailed analysis of a magnetic impurity that induces spin-orbit spin-valley coupling, providing explicit demonstrations of vertical spin transfer between valence bands.

Optimization methods are increasingly vital across numerous scientific and commercial domains. As the field expands, new approaches are being developed at a rapid pace, yet current open-source project management frameworks for optimization remain limited. This paper introduces LibOPT, a community-maintained library dedicated to providing open-source access to a broad spectrum of modern optimization techniques. Designed for flexibility, it enables the rapid and easy development of new solvers, rendering it an ideal platform for researchers to experiment with innovative methods. Additionally, the framework supports the rapid and simple creation of robust software applications for solving practical problems. By offering such a dynamic space for innovation, LibOPT aims to help scientific and engineering communities accelerate the development of new solutions and apply them to a wider variety of use cases.

This paper examines the transference degree, $\delta$, as introduced by D. C. Micale in his thesis, with respect to the uniform algebra $A(X)$ on a uniform algebraic variety $X \subset \mathbb{P}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}$. This involves exploring scenarios where $X$ is either smooth or contains singularities defined by specific codimension and degree constraints. Furthermore, several additional results concerning the transference degree are derived.

Internal symmetry groups defining particle properties face a crisis in non-commutative spacetime frameworks like the Moyal plane, as non-trivial elements of the corresponding star product induce significant challenges in constructing the internal symmetry group itself. Specifically, a conflict arises between the concepts of particles and internal symmetries: quantum particles experience a fundamental identity crisis in this environment.

This work demonstrates the capability of the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method (TPABTIC) for mapping charge transport in three dimensions within type II single-crystalline synthetic diamond. By exciting carriers deep within the bulk and monitoring their trajectories as they reach the surface, the technique reveals type II diamond's inherently anisotropic and depth-dependent charge transport characteristics. The resulting data aligns with theoretical predictions derived from drift-diffusion modeling.

Online hate speech poses a critical threat to individuals and communities worldwide, particularly in the form of misogyny, which endangers women and drives many to withdraw from the workforce due to shame and fear driven by social media hostility. Although automated detection systems for other categories of hate exist, no such specialized framework currently addresses the detection and community management of misogyny on Arabic platforms. Consequently, this study introduces the world's first multi-task approach dedicated to detecting and classing online abusive content targeting women on these platforms. The research utilizes two distinct datasets: one for binary classification and another for multi-label categorization. The proposed method employs a multi-layered perceptron to identify misogynistic content and a separate classifier to categorize the abuse into sub-types. Additionally, to address data scarcity affecting model performance, the authors apply transfer learning using the BERT-base-arabic pre-trained model. Results indicate that this hybrid approach achieves 99.0% accuracy on the binary task and 80.7% accuracy on the multi-label task, significantly outperforming previous methods. The authors further propose a set of recommendations for effective automated moderation of such content within online communities.

This paper investigates fractional backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) of delayed type featuring a delayed drift component and a postponed generator, alongside the associated forward stochastic differential equation (FSDE). The study addresses the existence, uniqueness, and dependence on parameters of solutions. Additionally, it establishes the generator's sensitivity with respect to parameters through the derivation of the Bernoulli principle for such equations.

We introduce a novel approach for training robust policies in dynamic environments by merging policy search with adversarial training. Specifically, the proposed method integrates the certainty of environment dynamics to create more reliable planning outcomes. By leveraging the conditional certainty of policy evaluation, the approach ensures better decision consistency even in the presence of model uncertainty. The resulting framework balances exploration and exploitation effectively and yields superior performance compared to standard Q-learning and policy search techniques when applied to stochastic systems. The solution addresses two primary challenges: the lack of closed-form approaches for specific cases and the absence of general solutions for such probabilistic environments.

We introduce a general framework for distributed computing that encompasses caching, distributed caching, and coded caching as specific instances. Within this context, the system state is defined as an indexed collection of file copies residing at cache nodes, where encoded strategies correspond to rules—either deterministic or randomized—that dictate how files are replicated. This approach addresses two primary challenges: (1) designing encoded strategies to minimize the system state's memory requirement, and (2) determining optimal system states to minimize network communication during content delivery. Although prior research has focused almost exclusively on minimizing memory for encoded strategies, this work focuses on the delivery efficiency of such systems. Specifically, we analyze delivery costs for caching, distributed caching, and coded caching. Our findings include a simple random encoding technique that achieves within a factor of $O(\log\log N)$ of the optimal delivery cost across all three contexts. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive theory for the single-subpacket downloading encoded caching problem, offering a strategy that provides the exact optimal delay and matching it with an optimal method for calculating the corresponding latency.

This paper introduces a version of PCD using univalent type theory, defined without quotient types or directed colimits by abstractly embedding Scott domains into a convenient category. This paper presents a commutative diagram that offers an alternative, fully explicit derivation of the constant term of an Eisenstein series for $GL(n)$ over rational adeles, a result originally established by Langlands using methods from algebraic group theory and available also in Godement's work. By relying entirely on discrete mathematics and avoiding analytic techniques where possible, we provide a primarily combinatorial proof. Where an element of linear algebra is required, it is used solely to handle the Weyl group; otherwise, the underlying proof structure remains a simple rearrangement summed across all permutations of the variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$.

This paper introduces a configuration-aware secure control approach for mobile robotic arms that integrates Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to ensure operator safety. Rather than formulating the safety assurance as a single high-dimensional optimization problem, our method leverages the arm's kinematic structure to create a set of low-dimensional, real-time feasible constraints. These constraints are derived by maximizing the safety margin while respecting the platform's kinematics and are solved in real-time within configuration space. While control-space formulations exist, they risk violating kinematic feasibility; alternatively, optimization in configuration space risks large control torques that can damage actuators. By addressing both issues simultaneously, our proposal enables safe operation of mobile robotic arms in human-interested settings. Simulation results for a mobile robotic arm validating this approach are included in the study.

Natural language processing is a broad field of computer science, and creating algorithms to concisely represent the core meaning of texts is a significant challenge within it. This study presents the use of graph-based structures to achieve text summarization through an extractive method. Graphs serve as an effective means for capturing text dependencies, and specific graph properties are identified as keys to selecting the most representative sentences. To identify these candidates, we employ sentence scoring, where each sentence is assigned a value based on its corresponding graph characteristics to gauge its importance. Finally, a subset of these candidate sentences is chosen to form the final abstract, and the approach is validated through various experiments.

We examine a nonlinear optical setup where two photons interact within a Raman resonance supported by a Bose-Einstein condensate. This configuration enables a binary quantum switch capable of a universal sign change for incoming wavefunctions. By modeling the system with a two-qubit quantum gate framework, we identify conditions that realize both the sign-flip component of a Pauli-X gate and a full phase accumulator for the computational basis states. While the system naturally produces a partial phase shift through its resonant behavior, we demonstrate that adjusting dispersion characteristics allows for precise realization of a complete sign flip on these specific basis states when subjected to a strong control pulse in the coupling region.

We prove that four distinct meromorphic maps from a complete K\"{a}hler manifold $M$ into projective space $\mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{C})$ avoiding a common target subvariety $X$ possess shared finite interpolation values, with these maps sharing no shared base points. Our findings also hold for certain infinite divergent meromorphic maps from $M$ to an algebraic variety $Y$, where four such distinct maps omitting a reference target variety $X$ exhibit identical interpolation properties and do not share any base points. Additionally, our extended Second Main Theorem yields insights relevant to the problem of uniqueness for systems of divergent holonomic maps.

Determining the number and nature of solutions to polynomial systems is a fundamental challenge with wide-ranging implications across mathematics and engineering. Contemporary approaches typically rely on numerical techniques initialized near an exact solution computed via Groebner bases or zero-dimensional polynomial ring structures. However, these methods often fail to detect all roots, especially in scenarios where initial guesses are distant from the target or precision issues arise. This study introduces a novel algorithm based on resultants that overcomes such limitations. By employing an adaptive strategy combining robust and precise numerical tactics, the proposed method effectively determines polynomial systems regardless of initialization proximity. Our results demonstrate that this approach successfully identifies all nontrivial loci in diverse test cases, uniting theoretical rigor with practical applicability.

Phenomenological studies of direct photons in Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\scriptsize{NN}}} = 200$~GeV reveal that their yields are consistent with expectations from $pp$ collisions scaled by the number of participating nucleons ($N_\text{part}$). Specifically, the $p_\text{T} > 5$~GeV direct photon transverse energy ratio ($R_{\rm direct}^{\gamma}$) remains flat across various centralities. This flat behavior indicates that the bulk of direct photons originate from hard processes outside the quark-gluon plasma. Consequently, any soft mechanism driving direct photon production in this energy regime does not appear to be modified by the formation of the QGP.

Moreover, this method supports localized resolution corrections, allowing high-quality visualization even when screen resolution is significantly greater than the standard one pixel-per-segment threshold.

This study presents a theoretical investigation into gamma-ray emission from internal shock shells produced by Galactic Shining Pair Stars (ShPSs). We identify the internal shock shell as the primary source of gamma-rays, contrasting it with conventional jet shells that form in supersonic star winds. As the ShPS moves at subsonic speeds relative to the surrounding stellar wind, the resulting internal shock generates emission from both gamma-ray to X-ray energies. The model predicts that the pulsar wind shock emits gamma-rays primarily in the GeV range, while the colliding stellar wind dominates the lower energies (soft gamma-rays and X-rays) within the shock structure. Consequently, the ShPS emits a dual-component spectrum: a peak near 1 GeV from the pulsar wind and a declining slope at lower energies from the stellar wind interaction. This specific spectral signature serves as a key diagnostic to distinguish ShPSs from Blazars, another major gamma-ray class. We further estimate that the Galactic ShPS population produces approximately 10% of the total gamma-ray output from the Galaxy.

Adverse weather conditions significantly impact human activities, prompting a need for accurate forecasting to mitigate negative consequences. While current weather categorization systems rely on extensive datasets and complex feature engineering, this study introduces the UNIBERSITY-based multi-class dataset, which encompasses 1,020 images of various weather types captured across diverse geographic and lighting environments. The paper also introduces a novel data augmentation strategy and presents two advanced Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures designed to handle these challenging variations. Experiments conducted on this new dataset, as well as evaluations using the existing public RES4Weather set, demonstrate that the proposed methods outperform state-of-the-art models. Additionally, to further validate the results across diverse scenarios, the study applies these techniques to a completely unseen image domain: underwater coral reef scenes.

This study investigates how various societal domains address climate change, specifically examining contributions from scientific, economic, and institutional sectors, as well as the standard of conduct surrounding the issue. Through a case study of these respective domains and the norms governing them, the paper aims to identify potential contradictions or alignments, assessing whether current behavioral norms are adequate given available contributions. Ultimately, the work proposes possible interventions to introduce desired changes.

This study introduces a virtual modeling and control framework for soft multi-fingered grippers, utilizing Koopman operator theory to derive a high-dimensional, linear, and time-invariant dynamical system. By employing this approach, the research establishes a bridge between a soft gripper's distinct physical configuration and its corresponding discrete-state dynamics. Furthermore, the research develops a simple, model-based regulation strategy to control these linear dynamical systems, achieving precise positioning with demonstrated experimental validation on a soft multi-fingered gripper.

Graphene represents a two-dimensional crystal structure composed of carbon atoms bonded in a hexagonal arrangement. By applying a twist along its thickness to this material, one generates a three-dimensional topological defect known as a dislocation. In this study, we apply Density Functional Theory (DFT) to analyze the atomic configuration and electronic characteristics of dislocations within monolayer and bilayer forms of twisted graphite. Our findings reveal that while the material's bandgap remains negligible, it exhibits non-trivial effects of topology on electron propagation.

We report the discovery of a new radio relic, J2102+6015, identified through observations from the GMRT and VLA. Situated at a cosmological distance of $z = 4.575$, this object is the most radio-loud shock structure found at such high redshifts to date. The source spans approximately 110 kpc in the object's rest frame, oriented roughly parallel to a local large-scale structure (filament) and exhibiting a bow-shock morphology. The bow shape indicates Bow Shock motion driven by the group's own outflow at a velocity of roughly 1,000 km/s. The source's luminosity ($L_{1400} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{24}$ erg s$^{-1}$ Hz$^{-1}$) and size are consistent with Mach shocks generated by a cluster moving at a transverse speed of roughly 1,000 km/s. The age of the bow shock is estimated to be around 100 million years, indicating that the radio emission likely began approximately 100 million years ago ($t_{\rm onset} \approx 10^8$ yr). Non-Silent Cell Lung Carcinoma (NSCLC) stands as the leading cause of cancer-related fatalities. Although its outcomes hinge on clinical factors like patient history and vital signs, as well as radiological features visible in CT scans, accurately predicting prognosis remains difficult due to these diverse data characteristics. To leverage both clinical and radiological information for prediction, we propose implementing a dual-stream architecture alongside strategies for data balance. Specifically, we employ separate networks to process radiological and clinical datasets, using a pre-trained ResNet 3D on CT imagery and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for time-series clinical records. To address the scarcity and disparity of this medical data, particularly regarding patient classifications, we apply Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) specifically for clinical variables. Furthermore, we integrate these streams via early fusion to create a comprehensive model for outcome forecasting. Testing against the LIDC-IDRI dataset confirmed our method's robustness, achieving an AUC score of 0.8155 on survival prediction tasks.

Reinforcement learning agents often struggle to capture the long-term value of specific actions due to the sparsity of immediate rewards, a flaw that frequently results in suboptimal performance. Although external knowledge has been utilized in prior research to address this limitation, we argue instead for constructing the most reliable agent-specific representation of the task as the case-specific goal action value. This approach, known as Goal-Action Value, serves as the primary driver for learning. Despite prior efforts, there has been no consolidated research providing a multi-dimensional evaluation of various reinforcement learning methods tailored to specific tasks. This paper offers a multi-aspect analysis of how different approaches perform across specific tasks and identifies several successful applications where external knowledge was effectively leveraged. Furthermore, we define the most pertinent forms of external knowledge for these specific tasks and highlight the most effective training strategies. Finally, we conclude by suggesting promising directions for future investigation.

Twitter Sentiment Analysis (TWSA) has become a vital resource for businesses seeking to gauge public opinion on products and services. Despite the maturity of various techniques for classical text sentiment analysis, challenges remain in applying them effectively to Twitter due to the platform's unique linguistic characteristics. This study introduces an Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework designed to overcome these hurdles. By employing time-series data from the Twitter API, the research demonstrates that incorporating temporal context enhances both the accuracy and effectiveness of the model. Empirical results confirm that this proposed approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an accuracy of 81.4% on the benchmark dataset.

We present an open-dimension dialogue framework centered on large pre-trained models, where a system engages in targeted discussions by adhering to specific role definitions. This study addresses the critical challenge of systematic role adherence within extensive dialogue contexts, a factor essential for maintaining system stability and generating engaging content. We detail our proposed architecture, which includes generating diverse responses aligned with the character's role through dual mechanisms: dedicated data collection involving various stylistic elaboration rules, and direct injection of role information into large language generation tasks. Evaluated through dialogue relevance and interest metrics across multiple role scenarios, our approach effectively demonstrates its capability to sustain stability and enhance user engagement.

Gravitational wave memory, a permanent displacement in detector arms, represents a significant nonlinearity within general relativity. We propose that this memory effect, generated by gravitational waves across various sources, could form a random backdrop detectable by current observatories like LIGO and Virgo. Characterized by a frequency-dependent amplitude of $10^{-21}\textup{ cm}$ at $1\textup{ kHz}$—yielding a $1\sigma$ signal per observation lasting $100\textup{ s}$—this effect would produce detections equivalent to an average of 3 events per day in regions where no actual events exist. Such "noise" could be distinguished from genuine astrophysical transients through standard time-frequency analysis techniques.

We introduce a novel SUSY-breaking mechanism driven by a complex scalar field, where its associated phase serves as both the order parameter and the susy-breaking mediator. This theory naturally facilitates baryogenesis through leptogenesis scales reaching the PeV range, as the generator of lepton number is linked to the susy-breaking sector. Additionally, the model produces a significant signature from the early universe: a gravatational wave spectrum peaking at nanohertz frequencies, which can be detected by future observatories such as the LISA mission. We further explore the conditions required for the formation of primordial black holes arising from this gravitational wave spectrum.

Emergent communications aims to prioritize efficient signal transmission over high data rates, focusing instead on ensuring the receiver understands the core semantic message. To achieve this semantic alignment between sender and receiver, we introduce a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates symbolic logic with learned representations for communication. Furthermore, we deploy a signaling game to establish shared semantics and promote meaningful interaction. Within this model, the sender utilizes emerging symbols enriched by neuro-symbolic features to encode information, while the receiver decomposes incoming data into these underlying symbols to retrieve their associated meanings for interpretation. To enhance communication reliability, we employ a transfer learning strategy to refine the sender's learning process. Our simulation results demonstrate that this proposed framework significantly boosts semantic understanding and communication performance.

Predicting new terms for existing synonyms is a critical challenge in Natural Language Processing (NPL). For instance, if a user defines "happy" as a synonym for "content" but only encounters "happy" in text, they cannot infer that the concept of being content also applies to the target noun phrase without further information. Recently, several Natural Language Processing models have been developed to address this challenge. However, most current approaches rely on training data that are both language and domain-specific, which limits their effectiveness when applied to data outside their training set. In this paper, we present a hybrid framework designed to mitigate this issue by integrating both language-specific and domain-known information. Our results demonstrate that our model performs more successfully than other existing approaches in accurately anticipating novel domain terms.

Active particles exhibit autonomous motion due to internal energy consumption, a behavior that diverges significantly from passive entities governed by thermal agitation alone. This distinction is especially pronounced for colloidal scales, where environment is filtered through the combined influence of thermal noise and self-generated activity. We investigate how energy consumption influences the dynamics of micron-sized colloids subjected to spatial activity gradients. Our findings reveal that while the effective temperature becomes entirely activity-dependent and spatially non-uniform in regions of varying activity, the actual colloidal velocity remains proportional solely to that local activity and shows independence from thermal noise or temperature. Furthermore, we derive an explicit analytical expression for the non-equilibrium structural distribution and compare our results with molecular dynamics simulations of hard disks. These computations confirm that the system's time evolution strictly adheres to a non-equilibrium form of the Boltzmann distribution, dictated entirely by local effective temperatures and activity profiles.

Discrete fracture network models are frequently built using implicit surfaces or level-set methods, which generate non-conforming mesh interfaces that pose significant challenges for standard finite element analysis. This study introduces the use of conforming multi-dimensional mesh fitting techniques alongside the Mimetic Finite Difference (MFD) approach to effectively address these complex geometries. We demonstrate that when combined with proper conformity, MFD offers a computationally efficient alternative to Finite Elements, delivering superior accuracy in simulating fluid flow across discrete fracture networks.

This study introduces innovative methods for maintaining cellular formations and avoiding collisions within drone swarms. We begin by formulating formation preservation as the point-set registration problem and proposing two specific solutions: one for general forms and another optimized for convex layouts. Both approaches rely on dividing initial formation points into groups based on a grid and performing registered transformations to minimize registration error. Following this introduction, we present original collision avoidance strategies that utilize the same centroid-based grid concept to define safe relative velocity bounds for drone movements. The effectiveness of our proposed algorithms and center-of-mass based velocity constraints has been verified through various simulation scenarios.

Let $S$ represent the Seidel matrix of a chain graph possessing $n$ vertices. This paper examines the range of $S$ and the number of its energy-accurate eigenvalue estimates, with particular attention to cases where the range is restricted to either $\{-1, 1\}$ or $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

This study addresses a regulated mean-field optimal control issue involving degenerate driven stochastic differential equations (DEEs), specifically focusing on the case where classical controls are constrained to a nonconvex and movable set. By reformulating the original non-degenerate problem into an equivalent one utilizing standard BSDFE and standard SDE, we leverage standard backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) theory to establish the existence of optimal controls. Subsequently, a dynamic programming method grounded in a novel partial differential equation (PDE) is employed to determine controls that satisfy regularity requirements within this framework. Finally, the theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations.

This study examines a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator defined as $D_{\alpha} = -i\sigma_{1}\partial_{x_{1}} - i\sigma_{2}\partial_{x_{2}} + V(x) + i\alpha(x)$ within $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. The components are given by $V(x) = (i\sigma_{3} + \sigma_{2})Q(x)$ and $\alpha(x) = i\sigma_{3}P(x)$, where $Q$ and $P$ represent matrix polynomials with matrix entries possessing finite degrees. This operator acts on two-component spinor functions $x = (x_{1}, x_{2}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ and involves Pauli matrices $\sigma_{1,2,3}$. Our primary objective is to determine the spectrum of $D_{\alpha}$ when $Q$ and $P$ correspond to elliptic finite-band torus potentials characterized by degrees $m$ and $n$, respectively. We demonstrate that the energy spectrum consists of $m+n$ finite bands separated by gaps. These findings are motivated by recent work establishing the spectral properties of Dirac operators in non-trivial gauge fields on the torus by Shigeyoshi and Kotake.

This paper introduces a two-tier heterogeneous Vehicular Ad-hoc Network (VANET) architecture, consisting of an infrastructure-based tier using Roadside Units (RSUs) and a vehicle-based tier utilizing Vehicle Relays (VRs). The VR tier aims to enhance data transmission reliability and extend network coverage by leveraging vehicles with sufficient battery reserves to act as mobile relays. We formally define the selection criteria for VRSs and establish the communication range in this novel structure. To analyze key metrics such as coverage probability, average network coverage, and average transmission energy, we employ Point Process theory alongside stochastic geometry. Furthermore, we derive closed-form expressions for coverage probability and average network coverage, with additional coverage probability results validated through Monte Carlo simulations.

Although Wikipedia serves as a highly reliable online encyclopedia, it contains articles of varying caliber, with some meeting quality standards only partially or not at all. To address this, we investigate automated methods for identifying low-quality content by analyzing the characteristic editing patterns associated with such articles. We find that certain behaviors, like extensive reverts and the application of protection measures, are more indicative of poor quality than others. Consequently, we propose two new metrics—the Average Edit Distance (AED) and the Edit Quality Score (EQS)—that quantify these patterns more effectively than existing approaches. Testing our methods involved calculating these scores for all Wikipedia articles across English, German, and Spanish language versions. We also developed a tagging system that leverages these scores to assign quality labels to unwritten-grammar-checked articles. Experiments on this synthetic dataset revealed that our proposed metrics significantly outperformed baseline techniques, with the resulting model achieving an F1 score of 0.7536 in English and between 0.7 and 0.8 in the European language variants.

Knowledge transfer forms the cornerstone of artificial intelligence, enabling newly developed models to benefit from previously learned capabilities. However, a significant limitation emerges when the source object is restricted to a black-box decision-based interface, which currently hinders applications such as deep learning in medicine or engineering. This study introduces a novel method to counter this constraint, enabling zero-shot knowledge transfer directly from black-box objects without needing their specific algorithms or theoretical frameworks. By constructing an internal surrogate model of the black-box system and applying rigorous convergence analysis, the validity of the approach is mathematically established. Furthermore, the methodology is validated and demonstrated across two practical domains: a synthetic engineering problem and a medical imaging task involving diagnosis.

Imitation learning has proven effective at accumulating display actions to enable agents to acquire complex behaviors. However, it necessitates a separate effort to record demonstrations, which limits its applicability to scenarios where such explicit recording is unfeasible. We introduce a framework that achieves mastery of intricate skills through collaborative multi-agent co-observance rather than imitation. By logging the full team display and utilizing self-supervised skills extraction to break down joint actions, our method eliminates the need for explicit human demonstration of specific individual skills. We validate this approach on three challenging physical tasks within the MuJoCo environment, showing performance that equals or surpasses current leading non-display-based co-op display methods.

We introduce a novel system designed to monitor the trajectories of hands and objects within an indoor environment, utilizing the Point-of-Cloud (PoC) representation to analyze how hands interact with items. This approach reconstructs these movements by combining results from two interacting PoC models: one representing the hand and another the object. Both are derived from the global PoC data capturing the entire scene, relying on a non-contact, untethered, and inexpensive sensor that operates without line-of-sight requirements between the operator and the target area. To determine the interaction mechanics, our method synchronizes the features extracted from both PoC models through point-to-point matching constraints alongside distance metric analysis. The proposed technique was validated using a dataset of 3D poses generated by the dynamic T-hand grasping scheme, demonstrating a capacity to accurately render hands in various positions while objects are manipulated.

We define and examine noncrystallographic tail-triangle C-groups of grades 4 with an interlacing count of two. Our analysis covers the determination of their fundamental groups, Poincaré polynomial structures, and specific properties of their associated tail C-groups. Additionally, their associated geometric tilings are defined and analyzed. Notably, our findings demonstrate the existence of exactly two such tail-triangle C-groups meeting these degree and interlacing constraints.

This paper introduces a deep learning method to estimate the robot's end-effector position relative to the depth camera without manual calibration. We frame this challenge as an inverse kinematics problem by formulating a neural network regression model that maps from the depth camera's field of view and orientation to the robot's joint angles. Since precise pre- and post-sensor calibration is unnecessary for our collected data, we employ an unsupervised calibration strategy to derive accurate intrinsics and extrinsics from the depth camera. We validate this model across two scenarios: a simulated robot arm and a real-world Franka Robotics arm. Our approach achieves higher precision than existing methods, particularly in simulated environments. Additionally, we open-source our calibration data and derived parameters to assist other researchers working with similar hardware configurations.

This work examines how treatment interference operates within a K-Nearest-Neighbors framework. We introduce a formalism to define interference and analyze the properties of a proposed estimator. Treatment effects are modeled as functions of a unit's neighbors, where neighborhood composition depends on a parameter $\alpha$ ranging from 0 to 1; as $\alpha$ approaches 1, this neighborhood increasingly aligns with the classical setup of K-Unit Contamination. We propose a new estimator for this model and demonstrate that it consistently estimates the treatment effect while possessing an established finite-sample variance. Furthermore, we show that our proposed estimator maintains coherence with both existing special cases and converges to our proposed method as $\alpha \to 1$. Consequently, we suggest a unified approach for constructing confidence intervals applicable to interference estimation across the full $\alpha$ spectrum.

The primary objective of the Stage-1 data for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) is to deliver robust cosmological constraint estimates, a goal that relies heavily on precise mass measurements of galaxy clusters. Achieving this requires processing vast datasets to determine lensing signals for millions of galaxies, a process susceptible to systematic errors that could compromise cosmological inference. This study introduces "ShapePipe," a novel software workflow designed to streamline the measurement of shapes for individual galaxies involved in cluster lensing analyses. We evaluate the performance of ShapePipe on UNIONS/CFIS data, a survey utilizing the $4m$ MAMA camera, to determine its efficacy. Our findings indicate that the pipeline delivers high-quality weak-lensing measurements, successfully achieving a signal-to-noise ratio of 5 for galaxies ranging from $10 < r < 20$ AB mag with an $r$-band surface density exceeding $10^5$ deg$^{-2}$.

The Kronecker–Weyl theorem establishes that the trajectory $\{n\alpha + b \pmod 1\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is equidistributed in $\mathbb{T} = [0,1)$ provided $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$ are such that $1, \alpha, b$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. This suggests that the long-term position of the orbit is uniformly random. A natural inquiry arises: how frequently does the orbit visit the open set $U \subset \mathbb{T}$ up to time $N$? The answer relies on the Diophantine characteristics of $1, \alpha,$ and $b$. Specifically, the frequency of visits $|\{n \le N : \{n\alpha + b\} \in U\}|$ converges to the Lebesgue measure $\mu(U)$ as $N \to \infty$ if and only if $b$ avoids Liouville criteria relative to $\{1\} \cup \{\alpha\}$. This criterion is optimal. These findings generalize to higher dimensions and are applicable to distinct problems in diophantine approximation, including those concerning well-approximable numbers.

This study examines the evolution of a dark vitality model within a universe governed by Tsallis holographic dark energy and a tsallis-based cosmological horizon, utilizing the tsallis-formulated Reidlinger–Anwyl–Fuji (RANF) holographic condition. We specifically analyze its behavior under the most intricate quintessence scenario and the associated holographic principle, demonstrating that this model can exist as a viable dark energy candidate. Additionally, we investigate its dynamical properties by formulating differential equations to represent this model's movement within the phase space, thereby exploring its implications regarding the Einstein-Gauss-Buettner (EGB) action principle in the context of a five-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Buettner action principle.

We present preliminary results from the LAMOST Time Domain Exploration project, which utilized photometric data from four K2 plates. Using the LAMOST Smart Data Service, we assembled a data set comprising 114 million measurements for approximately 34 million stars. Following quality control, we identified 11,841,310 variables, which were further classified as likely non-autovariates (non-AAVVs) based on the duration of their light curves. To validate these findings, we cross-referenced our list with the RAVEVarVar catalog and the Gaia RVDV variable list, confirming 94% and 96% of the sources respectively. This paper introduces TuRaN, a novel SRAM-based true Random Number Generator (RNG) that leverages the inherent unpredictability of SRAM initialization. While previous RNGs targeting SRAM vulnerabilities focused on cell yield discrepancies, this approach instead exploits variations in cell discharge duration caused by power domain voltage underecaling. By reading SRAM rows as the system operates at progressively lower voltage levels, a highly diverse dataset is gathered that effectively resists RNG attacks relying on standard modeling and extraction techniques. This strategy yields genuine entropy suitable for RNGs with a reported entropy rate of 2.4 bits per character and an efficiency reaching 94.6%. Additionally, the design ensures a high barrier against RNG compromise, achieving an information-theoretic security level of $2^{127.4}$.

This study introduces a new class of nonvolatile resistive memory devices engineered with a single molecular break junction as the active element and employing electrostatic single-electron switches (SEES) to control resistance. The proposed architecture combines the compact dimensions and high data storage density achievable through self-assembled monolayers with the inherent stability provided by SEES. Furthermore, the design ensures that resistance switching is mediated solely by electrostatic mechanisms, bypassing the need for electron tunneling through the switch structure. The paper presents a comprehensive model of a prototype device consisting of three gold nanoislands separated by two organic junctions, utilizing discrete and mean-field approaches to evaluate charge stability and the functional switching process. The analysis demonstrates that electrostatic charge stability can be maintained across the entire switching regime when molecules are chosen with appropriate energy level positions and when the constituent islands are dimensioned correctly.

We introduce a novel approach to the causal depiction of multi-loop Feynman diagrams. This method is universal, applying to integrands of arbitrary topological structure without requiring the loop integrals to be evaluated. The resulting diagrams are two-dimensional, with propagators rendered as lines and protons depicted as distinct nodes. A primary advantage of this visualization technique is its capacity to concisely and clearly illustrate the causal connections between various components of a diagram. The method's efficacy is confirmed through the presentation of the visual outputs for over 1,000 graph topologies multi-scale QED computations involving up to three loops.

This paper introduces a closed-form analytical formula representing the time-evolved state of a one-dimensional two-level quantum walk. By formulating the coefficients as a sum of explicitly defined complex numbers, we enable direct computation and offer greater insight compared to existing characteristic equations. Furthermore, we utilize this formula to derive a specific expression for the hitting probability of the walk. An application of our results is demonstrated for a system featuring a time-dependent Peierls phase, illustrating the method's utility.

This study explores equilibrium configurations for compact stars, including neutron and hybrid stars, by integrating the relativistic mean field (RMF) approach with mass density-dependent quark phase transitions derived from MIT bag and NJL models. We specifically examine how varying parameters linked to the quark deconfinement process influence the properties of these neutron and hybrid stars. Our analysis reveals that predictions for the maximum mass and radius of stable stars differ notably between the NJL and MIT bag model frameworks. Notably, our results indicate that increasing the critical density for quark deconfinement leads to an expansion of the range of stable hybrid stars and enhances their maximum allowable mass. Additionally, we address the stability of these stars in terms of both radial and strangeness oscillations.

We investigate slow and fast light phenomena within a quadratically q-deformed Carmeli-Laser (CML) system. By applying the quantum h-adiabatic approximation (QHA), our results demonstrate that both slow and fast light effects can be readily controlled via q-deformation and parameter tuning, with the observed changes in wave packet propagation directly reflecting the underlying optical dynamics. Additionally, we examine how the quantum characteristics of the initial mechanical state influence the magnitude of these light speed modifications, ultimately discussing the precision with which the q-deformation allows for slow and fast light control.

The 3D Dual-Rotors Model (DRM) offers a framework for analyzing Adverse R-Parity even states located above the 2N threshold. This paper investigates specific even states within the model's characteristic Adverse R-Parity (ARP) bands, which appear as the $K^{\pi}=1^{+}$ and $K^{\pi}=2^{+}$ sequences exceeding the $2N$ energy level. We demonstrate that states with $K=1$ in the DRM exhibit characteristics of ARB bands, providing the inaugural evidence of an ARB state in this specific even-spin sequence. Furthermore, we utilize the model to forecast the energies of $K=1$ and $K=2$ ARP bands up to spins $I=10$ and $I=12$ respectively, offering predictions that closely align with experimental observations.

Epitaxial strain, resulting from the mismatch in lattice constants between a film and its substrate, is a critical factor in controlling electronic and magnetic properties within heterostructures. In ultra-thin films, where intrinsic lattice mismatch values are amplified by the dominance of substrate-imposed epitaxial mismatch, this strain can be actively tuned through in-situ methods such as epitaxial buffer layers, growth on curved substrates, or epitaxial expansion/contraction driven by thermal effects, lattice transformations, or external fields. Consequently, researchers have successfully manipulated a range of phenomena—including carrier density, Fermi surface characteristics, carrier mobility, and magnetic ordering—in ultrathin structures through these strain engineering techniques. This collection of studies offers a comprehensive overview of experimental observations regarding both magnetic and electronic responses to strain in films as thin as two unit cells.

We introduce a quantum many-body model depicting a one-dimensional optical lattice shaken with an external laser, where a large cloud of atoms undergoes average laser cooling. This interaction with light generates a time-dependent term within the system's Hamiltonian, driving non-equilibrium dynamics that can be partially counteracted by the dissipation responsible for the cooling process. When the shaking intensity falls below a specific threshold, the system reaches a steady state characterized by a Gaussian distribution of atom positions and a quasi-adiabical evolution of the atoms. In this regime, we analyze the dynamical behavior of a single impurity atom interacting with the cloud, observing at low shaking intensities a dynamical phase transition in the impurity's occupancy statistics. Furthermore, we examine how these non-equilibrium effects influence the system's entanglement dynamics.

This study utilizes higher-order spectrum analysis to investigate dependencies within the cryptocurrency market. The results demonstrate that non-pairwise connections exist between coins, indicating that these complex, multi-entity interactions are more significant than traditional pairwise dependencies. Furthermore, these higher-order effects are not constant; they fluctuate based on the specific groupings of assets involved and are most pronounced during market crises. Consequently, modeling the trading dynamics of the digital asset landscape demands an approach that explicitly accounts for complex spectral dependencies involving multiple assets simultaneously.

This study examines the structural and thermodynamic characteristics of small hydrogen-water and hydrogen-sulfate acid droplets, specifically those comprising up to 10 molecules. Our methodology couples the correlated molecular dynamics technique with the density functional theory approach to treat electronic components. By incorporating these 0-point movements, our model achieves remarkable alignment between simulated sulfuric and water droplet free-energies and experimental measurements. Notably, these vibrational effects are essential for explaining the anomalous boiling point of water and the unusually high boiling point of sulfuric droplet formation. Furthermore, these 0-point motions significantly alter the propensity of water to form clusters, whereas such vibrational contributions are negligible for sulfuric acid droplet formation and droplet growth dynamics.

In the context of a compact group acting on a compact locally convex abelian topological group, this paper demonstrates that the space of group-equivariant non-expansive functions—subject to either bounded or non-expansive constraints relative to a given metric—forms a compact subset within the larger space of all bounded functions, when equipped with the topology of uniform convergence. This finding serves as a compact-group analogue to a well-known theorem by Banach. Furthermore, the study extends this result to anions involving amenable topological groups through the consideration of compact recognition pairs.

It is widely held that the success of deep learning relies on the implicit regularization provided by optimization algorithms, which naturally favor simple model solutions. We demonstrate that this conclusion rests on a flawed premise: simplicity alone cannot be used to identify the model that generalizes best. Instead, our analysis of generalization error as a function of geometric complexity reveals that model performance often improves with increasing geometric complexity, meaning the "simplest" model is not necessarily the optimal one for generalizing. Consequently, these findings suggest that other factors, such as explicit regularizers, play a more significant role in determining generalization than does simplicity alone. Our arguments apply broadly and are supported by rigorous mathematical reasoning, offering wide-ranging implications for how we understand model selection in deep learning.

We investigate flavor-changing neutral current processes involving down-type quarks, specifically focusing on decays to vector and scalar final states. By employing an analysis that relies solely on experimentally accessible observables, we derive model-independent constraints on the underlying Wilson coefficients. Experimental data from LHCb are used to determine these limits, which exhibit significant overlap with previous results obtained for $B\toK^{(*)}\ell^{+}\ell^{-}$. Furthermore, we propose an analytical framework that enables rapid, back-of-the-envelope estimations of the bounds derivable from any given dataset.

Automated essay scoring stands as a critical challenge in natural language processing, driven by the immense volume of grade reports required for grading in large-scale examinations. We introduce a novel data augmentation approach designed to empower transformer-based models for numerical rating prediction. By leveraging surface forms to create syntactically robust variations, our method maintains semantic consistency while multiplying training set size. Empirical results indicate that this strategy significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, particularly within the British English context of the BEA challenges, effectively reducing reliance on extensive synthetic data generation.

Marginal models, which are frequently utilized in practice, are not always interpretable. We introduce a class of marginal dependence models featuring closed-form solutions for both mean and covariance, applicable to blocks of data with binary values. These models extend the linear4x approach by imposing a multivariate t-distribution on the latent variables. We further demonstrate how to nest these multivariate t-distributions within broader stochastic volatility and factor models. We outline model specifications, implementation details, and results from simulations as well as applications to real-world datasets.

This research introduces a stochastic dynamic programming framework for dynamic treatment selection, specifically addressing opportunity distribution among individuals with varying potential levels and dynamic characteristics. We examine a multi-agent system where agents progress through a hierarchical ladder, making treatment decisions at each node to determine whether an agent advances to the next tier or remains stationary. Our primary objective is to determine a treatment assignment policy that maximizes the long-term count of agents reaching the top position, treating the unknown agents' features and underlying transition dynamics as unknowns requiring simultaneous estimation and optimization. We address this challenge using methods from dynamic contextual treatment selection, specifically targeting first-order optimality for the incentive scheme while providing theoretical guarantees on the convergence rates of our simultaneous learning and planning algorithm through rigorous analysis. The effectiveness of this approach is validated via numerical experiments, supported by additional insights from applications to social mobility and wage progression.

We introduce a modified version of the Monero blockchain featuring enhanced privacy and performance. By utilizing a "delegation" scheme to verify transaction amounts and the sum of inputs against outputs only, we ensure that high-velocity networks can support anonymous transacts at elevated throughput. We investigate the linear equation $Ax=b$ for a sparse matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ with sparsity $s$ and an input vector $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Assuming access to a black-box oracle that retrieves any entry of the target solution $x$ in constant time, we establish lower and upper bounds for the minimal number $s^*$ of white-box queries (which yield full solution vectors) required to resolve the problem. Our analysis covers four scenarios: (1) full knowledge of $A$ and $b$; (2) full knowledge of $A$ with $b$ accessed via an oracle; (3) $b$ obtained through an element-wise query (limited to $s$ queries); and (4) $b$ obtained through a vector-wise query (consuming one query). We demonstrate that for settings (1) and (2), the knowledge of $A$ provides no advantage, yielding $s^*= \Omega(m)$; this contrasts sharply with scenarios (3) and (4), where the vector nature of $b$ allows a knowledge advantage, resulting in $s^*= \Omega(\frac{m}{s})$. These findings indicate that, in the vector cases, $s^*$ represents the optimal sublinear complexity achievable by algorithms that rely on vector queries.

Modern data-driven and collaborative modeling approaches aim to harness available data for constructing accurate models of complex systems. Key challenges in this field include merging disparate data sources with varying degrees of trust, as well as formulating explicit trust between participants. To address these issues, our work focuses on two main problems: first, creating frameworks to integrate trust models and fuzzy sets into both data modeling and collaborative data analysis; and second, developing a technique for trust-aware federated learning that explicitly accounts for trust relationships among participants. In the former approach, our method produces locally trusting models that incorporate uncertainty, with subsequent analysis demonstrating how to jointly analyze these distributed models while respecting both trust relations and fuzzy constraints. For the latter, we outline a mechanism for trust-aware federated learning, complete with corresponding analysis to ensure the learning process respects the underlying trust structure between participants.

We introduce a novel approach to predictive security filtering designed for linear time-invariant systems subject to unstructured noise. The core goal is to develop a predictive estimator with the minimum possible gain, ensuring its transfer function remains stable. This method proves particularly valuable in safety-critical applications where enhancing noise reduction is constrained by the risk of introducing latency. The proposed framework generalizes the $H_\infty$ filter and aligns conceptually with the $H_2$ optimality principle operating under anti-aliasing conditions. A key advantage of this approach lies in its derivation via a two-space formulation, which guarantees a clear connection is maintained with the original problem space.

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) relies fundamentally on two security measures: vacuum decoys and full phase randomization. While Fagan et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 112, 08050 (2014)) previously demonstrated a QKD hacking strategy that evades detection under partial phase randomization, comprehensive analysis of the attack's limits across varying levels of randomization had been missing. This study addresses that gap by numerically investigating such attacks across the entire decoy-state protocol spectrum for single-photon, multi-photon, and vacuum states. Our results align closely with the extreme case of no randomization found earlier, suggesting that threats arising from incomplete phase randomization in decoy-state QKD are minimal.

This paper examines how different pre-training corpora within language models (LMs) influence the efficiency of in-context learning (ICL). We investigate three primary questions: the differences in performance across LM variants equipped with varying ICL tasks, the specific training data requirements for optimizing particular tasks, and the role of high-quality data versus task-relevant data. Our findings reveal that while larger model capacities generally enhance performance, pre-training data has a profound effect on ICI. We observe that incorporating task-relevant information into pre-training corpora significantly boosts performance, surpassing the gains made solely by expanding model size or adding more generic data. Furthermore, our results indicate that pre-training quality matters, yet relevant contextual knowledge is superior.

We investigate the fragmentation and expansion dynamics of cold clouds injected from active galactic nuclei into hot intracluster media, focusing on how internal structure, thermal states, magnetic fields, and the surrounding environment influence their lifetimes. Using three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we modeled fragments both adiabatically and with radiative cooling, varying initial temperatures from $10^4$ K to $10^6$ K and magnetic field orientations randomly or aligned with gravity. Our results indicate that radiative cooling drastically shortens cloud lifespans, reducing them by an order of magnitude compared to an an adiabatic scenario. While cooling rates are generally independent of initial temperature, alignment of magnetic fields with gravitational forces can extend survival times by up to 50\%. We further assessed interactions between cooling and expansion, finding that expansion can delay collapse by 20\%-30\% in highly cooled clouds. These findings suggest that internal cloud structure and thermal evolution are critical in determining destruction timescales, with significant implications for cooling flow models and feedback mechanisms within galaxy clusters.

This study examines Charge Parity (CP) violation in $b$- and $c$-hadron decays. The review covers the theoretical framework of mixing, neutral kaon decays, and tree-level violations, alongside model-dependent scenarios. It further presents data from the California Institute of Technology's Collider Detector at Fermilab (CDF) experiment alongside world averages regarding beauty charm decays.

By applying the bosonic tough string vertex with Lax operators, we derive tree-level scattering amplitudes for various closed superstring theories, covering both Neveu-Schwarz and Ramon sectors. Our findings demonstrate that these amplitudes align perfectly with established standard results across all known superstring frameworks. Furthermore, leveraging this novel vertex, we revisit closed string scattering within the type IIB system and the open string in type I. We present explicit computations for the first two transverse polarizations in type IIB closed strings as well as one polarization in type I closed strings, alongside calculations for multiple polarizations involving the open strings in type I. Ultimately, these computed results confirm agreement with conventional amplitude formulas, and we discuss the extension of the Gross conjecture regarding the precise relation between type I and open string type I theories.

Driven by the rapid growth of data traffic and evolving 5G use cases—including massive machine-type communications (mMT C) and supergigabit roaming communications (m2C and massive) - network operators are increasingly compelled to adopt Self-Organizing Network (SON) capabilities. These capabilities are essential for reducing operational expenditures (OpEx) and ensuring efficient, high-quality service delivery. This paper outlines the fundamental network management functions required to enable a robust and effective SON ecosystem, analyzing their specific contributions across the three primary SON categories: Self-Planning, Self-Configuration, Self-Optimization. We further address critical challenges inherent in integrating these processes with other networking technologies, specifically focusing on Non-Territory Based (NTB) and Software-Defined Networking (SDN). Ultimately, the study demonstrates how these emerging frameworks can bolster SON deployment within 5G cellular environments, enhance overall network performance, and sustain future growth.

This study introduces a deep neural network method for generating text-independent speech synthesis without relying on any text representations. Using only audio recordings, the model creates a vocabulary of perceptual units and trains a neural network to synthesize audio from unit sequences. We designate these proprietary units as "auditory icons," distinguishing them from traditional acoustic or phonemic alternatives by their role in reducing both data annotations and computational complexity. An experimental assessment using the AudioSet dataset indicates that these new models achieve comparable quality to conventional approaches while demanding significantly lower amounts of labeled data and computational resources.

Motion planning is a critical issue in robotics, and this paper proposes a data-driven method to enhance planning efficiency. We frame efficiency as planning duration and address it as a multi-objective optimization problem. Objectives include minimizing total duration, total energy consumption, and the count of optimization phases. By formulating these goals as a multi-objective optimization task, various balanced solutions can be generated to suit varying operational needs. Focusing on efficiency and phase count, we derive an efficient two-phase strategy. The first phase estimates travel duration using limited data via a probabilistic model, while the second minimizes energy consumption constrained by that estimated time. To tackle the resulting difficulty, a multi-objective optimization solver is employed, yielding diverse solutions with different trade-offs. To further accelerate computation, we introduce a data-informed programming framework. This incorporates problem-specific relaxations into McCormen envelope conditions, enabling a high-performance solution for this otherwise challenging task. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We examine the fundamental constraints on the probabilistic conversion between quantum states by demonstrating that if a target state ensemble is not a convex mixture of clones of the source ensemble (denoted as $\mathcal{S}$), then no transformation strategy can be entirely successful in converting the former to the latter, even when using only quantum operations that preserve the trace. Furthermore, we show that under specific conditions, even approximate transformations cannot yield results with non-negligible probability. These findings elucidate the limitations of quantum error correction strategies and state scrambling protocols, whereas our upper bounds on transformability also yield novel proofs of cloning limitations for pure and mixed states as well as new proofs of the impossibility of increasing quantum entropy.

This work presents a detailed mathematical analysis of incompressible inviscid fluid dynamics within a cylindrical vessel that functions as a simple pendulum, focusing on specific sloshing modes. By employing the method of matched asymptotic expansions, we derive an ordinary differential equation governing the vessel's amplitude. This derived equation aligns with the dynamics of an anharmonic pendulum featuring a double well potential. Consequently, we analyze stability characteristics and compute bifurcation diagrams for the system. Finally, our findings are compared against experimental data obtained for actual pendulum-style coffee cups.

Decentralized learning faces significant hurdles when dealing with data non-independence, communication channel impairments, and heterogeneity among nodes. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel robust learning framework that combines distributionally robust optimization with decentralized learning. By integrating a Kullback-Leibler divergence constraint, our approach ensures a learning guarantee against data variations, network topology irregularities, and communication noise. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the proposed learning algorithm converges to a neighborhood of the global optimal solution, with the radius of this neighborhood depending on data robustness parameters, topological heterogeneity, and communication noise. Furthermore, we teach other nodes in a decentralized setting, showing that our teaching algorithm outperforms standard generalization methods by offering stronger theoretical guarantees regarding theoretical performance. Extensive experiments validate the theory and illustrate that our learning algorithm achieves superior results on both synthetic datasets and real-world applications.

We investigate particle production in relativistic nuclear collisions through the lens of hydrodynamic evolution, specifically examining how an initial non-equilibrium state influences final multiplicity. Our analysis reveals that generating a high final multiplicity necessitates a high initial energy density; however, equating this to microscopic sources like "microbursts" is misleading. This study examines the dynamics of jet-driven outflows using 1D hydrodynamic simulations. We modeled a protostar emitting a high-velocity jet, investigating how the resulting low-velocity outflows vary with jet Mach number ($\mathcal{M}$). Results indicate that low-velocity outflows consist of two components: an inner region dominated by jet material and an outer region shaped by a high-velocity jet. Basket trials represent an emerging clinical trial format intended to identify treatments for rare diseases, typically by grouping them into baskets sharing a presumed common treatment effect. These designs employ two approaches: either comparing a shared experimental arm against distinct control groups per basket, or utilizing multiple experimental groups compared against a single control. However, uncertainty often surrounds whether a single treatment truly benefits all baskets, creating a need to borrow historical or hypothetical data. This study proposes a Bayesian method for sample size calculation in basket trials that explicitly accounts for the possibility of borrowing. The method's performance is validated through a simulation exam under various scenarios, demonstrating that the procedure is effective and can be readily implemented basket trial proponents.

This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to enhance trajectory precision in high-precision motion systems by addressing position errors caused by nonlinearities and external disturbances. The core mechanism involves a deadbeat control strategy that achieves rapid system stabilization through the sequential shutting of loops, supplemented by an LPV system model enhanced with anti-windup measures to mitigate integral accumulation and prevent actuator saturation. While these design choices serve to boost system robustness, they are also examined against the system's anti-disturbance capabilities. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through both simulations and experimental testing focused on a trajectory following task within a motion control framework.

Achieving robust, model-free partial-to-partial registration is crucial for facilitating partial-to-full alignment and remains a significant challenge in point cloud processing. Current deep learning methods typically target complete-to-complete registration or depend heavily on full surface coverage, often ignoring shape priors and failing to generalize to novel shape pairs due to invariance to large rigid transformations. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework, PRNet, designed specifically for partial-to-partial registration. We address three core challenges inherent to this domain: handling shape priors, managing large rigid invariance, and resolving ambiguity during feature extraction and alignment. To overcome these hurdles, PRNet employs self-guided learning that utilizes both the query and support fragments to facilitate feature encoding and subsequent alignment. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms both previous deep learning approaches and state-of-the-art model-free techniques. Furthermore, ablation studies and comparisons with alternative strategies confirm PRNet's superior generalization capabilities and robustness.

The collider landscape is entering an era of precision, offering enhanced opportunities to investigate phenomena beyond the Standard Model. One such phenomenon, the SM instability, could serve as a doorway to new physics. This work outlines a framework at colliders to detect this instability and assess its significance. Taking into account that the instability's signature evolves with center-of-mass energy and takes several forms, we determine the optimal experimental setup to identify it. We conclude that a facility with a high luminosity fixed-target configuration is best positioned to detect the SM instability.

This study presents a new approach for time-resolved spectral inversion that utilizes a forward-optimal control theory. Reshaping the standard state estimation problem, we formulate it as a boundary-value problem derived from the Hamiltonian of optimal control, resulting in a nonlinear, non-degenerate eigenvalue problem. Within a trajectory framework, this formulation enables the determination of optimal estimates for information carriers by applying the state estimator alongside a numerical framework. We demonstrate this methodology using simulated data representing ultrafast optical absorption in water, a scenario where state convergence and the precise timing resolution of solutes are analyzed.

Witten proposed a method to derive meson distribution amplitudes from their Bethe-Salpeter wave functions, a framework we have used to evaluate distribution amplitudes for $D$- and $D_s$-mesons. In this study, we extend that analysis to cover mesons with spin 2 ($2^-$), specifically the $D^*$ and $D_s^*$ states. The resulting distribution functions $H$ and $A_1$ are determined by the components of the $B$ and $C$ terms found in the corresponding Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. We further investigate how these distribution amplitudes behave at high momentum scales and obtain numerical results for the associated parameters $H$ and $A_1$.
