Existing work in zero-shot learning for audio classification is limited to single-task scenarios and does not tackle multi-task settings. This research introduces a new framework for multi-modal, zero-shot distributed learning with new audio categories. The method utilizes multiple datasets to define characteristics of both known and unseen sound classes, a process supported by a unified representation model that links seen and unseen concepts through provided labels. The proposed system for multi-task, zero-shot distributed audio classification has been tested on the standard dataset. The results demonstrate that this approach outperforms current best practices in multi-task, zero-shot audio classification by a significant margin.

This paper introduces an all-encompassing framework for evaluating multiqubit entanglement, defined by an optimizable global parameter that generalizes existing measures found in the literature. With this formalism, we have established an optimal structureassessed GHZ state, confirming previous findings that asymptotic states of trapped ions constitute entanglement optima. Furthermore, this structure allows for an efficient calculation of entanglement in high-dimensional systems; applying this method to "Orbital Angular Momentum" (OAM) photons, we identified specific three-partner states that achieve entanglement optimality and are structurally analogous to the Bell-diagonal GHZ state. Additionally, we demonstrated that certain two-qubit states, when extended to qutrits, achieve structural entanglement optimality, notably including the "W-state"-like states featuring distinct single-excitation properties.

This study introduces a channel assessment framework for Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS)-aided Multiple-Input Multiple-Output systems serving multiple devices. The approach utilizes a cascaded channel model to separately estimate IRS-to-User and User-to-IRS channels, enabling compact representation of phase coupling across reflecting elements. To minimize hardware complexity, the framework proposes calculating precoding matrices and computing phase shifts using only one radio frequency (RF) chain per access point and passive element. Simulation results confirm that the suggested method enhances sum-rate performance while significantly reducing implementation complexity.

This research analyzes U.S. regional news coverage of COVID-19 using data from 1,055 outlets, examining the timing and quantity of articles alongside the volume of tests, infections, and fatalities. It further investigates the link between news consumption and attitudes toward the virus. Findings indicate that, relative to the pace of the pandemic, regional news outlets produce a higher volume of COVID articles than national media. Notably, the U.S. news cycle is punctuated by distinct spikes in coverage, with the first major surge occurring in April 2020. The study observes a strong correlation between levels of news consumption and news production, as well as between audience intake and public perceptions of the virus's risk. However, these relationships are subject to significant seasonal fluctuations.

Neural networks are increasingly recognized for their ability to simulate human cognitive processes, specifically regarding memory and its role in problem-solving. This study examines whether equipping a neural network with Hebbian associative memory enhances an agent's capacity to master the "counting task" compared to a model without such mechanisms. The research confirms that integrating this learning rule significantly accelerates task acquisition. Furthermore, the analysis delves into the specific contribution of remembered information within an agent's computational trajectory.

Filter data structures are widely used to manage massive datasets efficiently. Among the most renowned are the Bloom filter and Cuckoo filter, though both suffer from limitations regarding space usage and filtering speed. This paper introduces a superior, space-speed optimized third-generation filter built upon xORSources—linear sources where elements are randomly assigned to buckets using xORSources—This novel structure offers a balanced improvement in performance metrics compared to previous approaches. We provide a rigorous analysis of the filter's time and space complexities, as well as its accuracy, supported by datasets of various types and scales. Our experimental results validate the structure's effectiveness, demonstrating significant gains in speed and size; specifically, we achieve a 30% reduction in data footprint and a 30% acceleration in query processing relative to the state-of-the-art MURMAP-based filter design.

This document outlines several connections regarding convex geometry within affine algebraic structures. Let $G$ denote an algebraic group acting with a complete, affine variety $X$. In this setting, $\text{Conv}(X)$ signifies the collection of all $G$-convex functions on $G\times X$. We establish that there exists a group action of $\text{Conv}(X)$ on $G$, identifying $\text{Conv}(X)$ as a subgroup of the group of algebraic transformations on $G$. Furthermore, we demonstrate a correspondence linking the group $\text{Conv}(X)$ to the group of algebraic subgroups of $X$ that are "convex," as defined by certain geometric properties. Additionally, we examine the structure of $\text{Conv}(X)$ when $G$ is taken to be the special linear group $\text{SL}_n$.

This study establishes a causal link between an anticipated market trend and current trade activity, demonstrating how future activity influences the present. To achieve this, we first construct a new metric called "Market Trend," representing the aggregate direction of price shifts, which is computable in constant time per trade using our proposed structure. This structure stores the cumulative product of the trend and trend-reverse factors—each defined as step functions relative to their respective thresholds. We then analyze the trade sequence to extract this metric empirically and statistically validate its predictive capabilities. Specifically, we demonstrate that the standard linear regression model significantly outperforms simpler models in forecasting market direction, providing robust statistical evidence of the data's properties and the metric's future-oriented effects.

This study introduces FLVoogd, a robust federated averaging framework that maintains integrity by preserving the confidentiality of local model updates while resisting various attacks. Updates from federated learning models are vulnerable to reconstruction attacks, which can expose sensitive data such as image pixels; consequently, we designed a new privacy-preserving commitment protocol to ensure update authenticity. Additionally, to guarantee stability against malicious participants, we developed a secure commitment protocol tailored for the federated Voogd setting. This framework offers both improved security and enhanced privacy while requiring minimal modifications to the standard federated averaging process. Experimental results demonstrate that FLVoogd successfully defends against multiple attack vectors and successfully restores data privacy during the mitigation of reconstruction attacks.

While Sim2EeND (simulation-to-end-to-end navigation) research has largely concentrated on optimizing simulation parameters to maximize real-world performance transfer, this study takes a contrasting, analysis-driven approach. We investigate how simulation-to-real reality divergence actually impairs generalization and demonstrate that these effects can be predicted through specific image gradient metrics. Crucially, these metrics function as viable proxies for real performance, enabling the formulation of constraints that bridge sim2real gaps with higher reliability than current proxy metrics offer.

Deepfake technology utilizes artificial intelligence to synthesize convincing forgeries by swapping faces or manipulating media content. As creative AI tools continue to evolve, producing increasingly realistic deceptive outputs, there is an urgent need for robust detection methodologies. This paper presents a comprehensive study of the end-to-end pipeline for both creating and detecting deepfakes across three primary domains: video, audio, and face clones. The authors analyze current state-of-the-art models within each category and evaluate their performance based on real-world data. Additionally, both advanced and accessible AI models are made publicly available on a dedicated GitHub repository to foster further research and development in this critical field.

The study of sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets with temperate climates remains a major focus in exoplanet research, as their internal structures and compositional makeup are often ambiguous. This uncertainty stems from the fact that their deep interiors can harbor vast oceans concealed beneath a supercritical layer, a configuration that differs significantly from the conventional model of a rocky core, metallic mantle, and silicate crust. We propose that a supercritical buffer zone can exist within these planets, where gas solubility equilibria diverge from standard thermal equations of state. This hidden layer's signature is imprinted on the observed transit curves, creating anomalies such as "bumps" or "dips" that reveal underlying compositional details. We introduce a new methodology to quantify these features, offering a pathway to distinguish between solubility-controlled phases and those defined by traditional gas thermodynamics. Applying this approach to the HD 219134 b system, our analysis indicates that the planet's interior likely consists of a supercritical layer situated atop a core composed of silicates and potentially metallic materials.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are recognized as a promising framework for neuromorphic computing due to their efficiency, high throughput, and low power usage. Although recent advancements in training methodologies have enhanced their performance, challenges remain in achieving biologically realistic operations. This work introduces a novel bio-feasile learning approach for supervised training of SNNs, designed to overcome current limitations. By integrating spike-based Hebbian rules for weight updates with an anti-Hebbian mechanism to induce spike decorrelation, we enhance temporal representation within the network. Additionally, by leveraging the temporal coding scheme, our method eliminates the reliance on artificial activation functions, thereby aligning more closely with biological neural processes. Experimental results demonstrate that this learning rule is as effective as contemporary state-of-the-art techniques for achieving high accuracy. Furthermore, when evaluated against recent methods designed to maximize co-spikes for enhanced efficiency, our method yields superior performance on various benchmark tasks.

This document presents the findings of the "Out-of-Context" challenge, an initiative designed to test model robustness by deliberately removing instructions, such as through the erasure of prompt headers. To address potential issues where a language model "modes down" and fails to follow any commands due to the absence of explicit authority in the input, we also included a "Find The Needle" sub-task. This task requires identifying the scarce instruction amidst non-instructional text. The text concludes by outlining key observations and offering suggestions for addressing the challenges posed.

This paper addresses a sequential identification and isolation (SICI) framework where a system's true state is only partially accessible due to random occurrences of state masking. The objective is to detect adaptive thresholds for switching systems while reliably estimating the underlying state despite these masking events. To achieve this, we develop novel limit-theorem results for the Least Mean Squares (LMS) and Maximum Likelihood (ML) approaches within the partially Observed Markovian State Space (pOMSS) framework. Furthermore, we propose an Adaptive ML (AML) method capable of simultaneously determining threshold values and performing sequence estimation. Under specific regularity conditions, our analysis demonstrates that the AML-based strategy achieves a linear expected detection delay and maintains a zero worst-case false alarm count. Simulation results confirm the efficiency and performance of the proposed method across various SICI scenarios featuring state masking.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of 12 dwarf galaxies, analyzing 120 stars with ages exceeding 10 billion years and metallicities ($Z$) ranging from $-3.0$ to $-1.0$ dex. Our work focuses on the evolutionary tracks of alpha elements (O, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti) and iron, alongside iron peak elements (Cr, Mn, Co, Ni). The observed O/Mg and Si/Mg ratios align with predictions from standard core-collapse supernova (CCSN) models. However, the Al/Mg ratio is significantly lower than expected, suggesting that either a significant fraction of aluminum was produced in neutron star mergers (NSMs) or that early galactic chemical evolution (CE) was shaped by the delayed enrichment from Type Ia supernovae (SNIa). We further examine variations in Ce/Ca and Ce/Ca to test whether the dwarf galaxies explored here exhibit distinct abundance patterns compared to those found in the Milky Way's satellites.

Let $G$ be a profinite group; this work introduces $\mathbf{hG}_+S$, a homotopy action spectrum featuring a continuous $G$-action. For an arbitrary coefficient ring spectrum $R$, we define the cohomology theory $H^*_hG(R)$. Assuming $G$ is abelian, we demonstrate that $H^*_hG(S^0)$ corresponds to the inverse of the Adams representation of group ring cohomology $H^*G(\mathbb{F}_p)$. For any profinite extension $1\to N\to{N}{\to}G\to1$ with finite, nilpotent domain subgroup $N$, we establish the transitivity of the theory, yielding an isomorphism between $H^*_hG(\cdot)$ and $H^*_hG(N)(\cdot)$.

Building accurate data extraction models for visually complex documents demands extensive, high-cost labeling using visual-language architectures. To address this, we introduce PROMETHEUS, a multi-stage framework that leverages both human expertise and automated capabilities to drastically cut labeling expenses while maintaining high performance. Our system first employs human annotators to label only sparsely selected representative samples. Subsequently, a trained model pre trains on these inputs to generate predictions for other documents. Any discrepancies between the model's suggestions and actual values are highlighted for final human confirmation. We tested this approach across two real-world extraction tasks involving diverse document layouts; results demonstrate that PROMETHEUS successfully replaces traditional full-human annotation with our proposed hybrid method, achieving comparable model performance at just 20% of the original labeling cost. Results further reveal that fully human-verified hybrid data enhances the model's ability to identify inconsistencies, ultimately leading to superior performance compared to scenarios where no human verification of generated data occurs.

Indium antimonide (InSb) and indium arsenide (InAs) are lattice-matched to europium sulfide (EuS), yet only the former supports a magnetic superexchange interaction across the EuS/semiconductor interface. Using *ab initio* calculations, we show that for both materials, lattice mismatch generates two stable interface configurations: one where europium sits above semmetallic (m) indium, and another above (c) central indium. We find that in the (m) case, hybridization between europium d and semiconductor p orbitals is suppressed for magnetic superexchange to occur. Training deep neural networks (DNNs) on data centers has historically been constrained by hardware capabilities, a bottleneck that necessitates learning model compression techniques to achieve efficient deployment. While research often targets reducing DNNs' memory footprint or speeding up inference, the training phase itself remains largely under-explored as a primary performance constraint. We introduce a new hardware-accelerated training compression framework that significantly reduces the memory requirements for DNN training. By applying structure-preserving pruning to compress the network architecture, we simultaneously reduce the storage needed for Pruned Weights (PW) and intermediate Pruned Weights (PP), which constitute the majority of training memory usage. To handle the resulting non-pruned activation data efficiently, we design a new compression algorithm based on quantization that is tailored specifically for this scenario. Furthermore, we develop a coordinated compression strategy that optimizes the balance between pruned, non-pruned, and weight storage to maximize accuracy and performance. Experimental results on extensive datasets demonstrate that our method achieves a 2.5x reduction in training memory with negligible accuracy loss, enabling the successful training of large-scale models like ResNet-152 and YOLOv2 on consumer-grade graphics cards.

We expand upon Ognjanov's modal complete lambek calculus with modal operators, adapting it for non-associative, distributive orderings. Notably, despite the absence of an associativity rule, a rule of modal contraction can still be demonstrated.

Gravitational waves generated by neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) mergers represent a significant source within the gravitational wave spectrum, expected to occur at a rate comparable to binary black hole mergers. Unlike black hole systems, NS-BH mergers allow for the emission of significant post-merger signals, which provide essential insights into the equation of state for nuclear matter, the properties of quark-gluon plasma, and other critical nuclear physics parameters. This study introduces a deep learning method designed to isolate and characterize these post-merger signals, demonstrating high efficacy in detecting and analyzing them.

"Transiting the star TOI-5542, the newly discovered exoplanet TOI-5542 b is a Hot Jupiter with a remarkably flat transit profile, indicating an inclination near 90°. Spectroscopic measurements of the system's radial velocity reveal the planet's minimum mass at $M_{\rm min} = 0.82^{+0.16}_{-0.15}\,\rm{M_{\rm J}}$. Spectroscopy also establishes a metallicity of $[{\rm{Fe/H}}]=-0.45\pm0.12\,{\rm dex}$ for the host star, which is notably low. Consequently, this system represents the second exoplanet host star with a determined but metal-poor metallicity, challenging the widely accepted correlation between planetary masses and stellar abundances. Additionally, the estimated system age of $7.1^{+6.2}_{-2.9}\,{\rm dex}$ years suggests that forming a gas giant in a chemically metal-deficient environment may be an ancient process."

Utilizing a primal–dual approach, we derive performance bounds for choice procedures implemented by agents facing Markovian environmental uncertainties and facing limitations on their selection actions. We introduce a methodology for constructing a dual representation of these procedures, contingent upon the imposition of a specific continuity constraint on the resulting representation. Subsequently, we establish both necessary and sufficient conditions regarding the existence of such procedures that satisfy these bounds. Finally, our existence criteria are applied to investigate two specific domains: (1) the investigation of constrained, myopic choice mechanisms, and (2) a constrained extension of the standard Thompson sampling procedure.
This paper outlines an approach to identifying handwritten mathematical notation, outlining both the advantages and limitations of deep learning methods for this notational recognition.

We offer a physical demonstration of the Bialynicki-Birula decomposition, which is applied to demonstrate the hard resolution of the natural operation of the cohomology of projective space. Furthermore, in the context of complex geometry, we utilize this derivation to revisit the \od R^+ scalar curvature flow.

Interactions among agents in intricate networks form the basis of complex system behaviors; however, these interactions are often treated as static or random, ignoring their inherent variability. This study investigates how interaction variability influences interaction processes and agent states by analyzing both artificial network models and actual data. We introduce the concept of an interaction matrix that quantifies interaction intensity, variance, and recovery rates, then apply random matrix theory to establish that various variability and recovery rate combinations yield a universal probability distribution for interaction durations. Furthermore, we utilize statistical analysis of real-world contact patterns to characterize interaction variability, assessing its impact on agent states through susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) and similar dynamical frameworks. Results indicate that interaction variability impacts system dynamics, with agents recovering more rapidly during shorter interactions than during prolonged ones.

This study introduces a novel actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm, termed "Deep Hamiltonian Policy Gradient" (DHGP), designed to tackle continuous control tasks. By integrating the Metropolis Heat Bath (MCMC) method, our approach enables the exploration of broader state and action spaces, offering significant advantages in the early stages of training. The proposed method, which combines MCMC sampling techniques with reinforcement learning, has been tested on various benchmarks from the OpenAI Gym suite. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this new algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning methods during training.

Drawing on the sieve methods of Eratosthenes and Goldbach, we establish the existence of a prime pair with minimal possible gap, effectively providing support for the twin prime conjecture. As a direct application, we prove the existence of primes \(p\) and \(p'\) such that \(|p-p'| = 2\cdot10^{12}\), addressing Miller's (1999) challenge.

This research introduces a layered navigation architecture designed to integrate diverse sonar technologies within a unified framework. A central Nucleus module manages data from multiple front-end sensors, handling both pre-processing and post-processing operations. It supplies blended sonar data to upper system modules, enabling the use of unified processing modules for various networking environments. Blending mechanisms, implemented through distinct pre and pre-collision handling processes, enhance the data quality for subsequent analysis. This paper specifically examines the design and functionality of these immediate blending processes, outlining how they improve data reliability before further processing.

Nereid, Neptune's third-largest moon, possesses a water ice surface heavily coated in dark, reddish contaminants, comparable in composition to the material found on Pluto's Nifedley Regio. Although Nereid's water ice exhibits significant spectral reddening and lower albedo than those traits are typically seen on Pluto's water ice, these observations can be replicated by a mixture of Nifedley and Sputnik Planitia ice components. Ground-based infrared spectroscopy of Nereid reveals that its water ice shows reddening and reduced albedo relative to those found on the dwarf planet. To address this, we developed a global model of the Nifedley ice component, which is characterized by a complex mixture of volatile ices (such as N₂, CH₄, and CO) mixed with silicate dust. This same Nifedley ice model was then applied to Nereid, but a pure version of it fails to fully match the observed spectral characteristics of the moon. Instead, our results indicate that Nereid's water ice is a complex mix containing various volatiles (specifically CH₄ and CO) and dust grains, which creates spectral properties distinct from those of pure Nifedley ice.

Let $T_n$ denote the set of all $n \times n$ lower triangular matrices with entries from a field $K$. This study examines the affine and projective surfaces defined by a homogeneous equation $f(T)=0$, where $T \in T_n$ and $f$ is an irreducible polynomial in $K[x]$. Our analysis specifically focuses on the case where $f(x)=x^r-x$.

The user has provided a paragraph from a mathematical paper, likely involving set theory and specifically discussing "Pawlikowski's theorems," "Tuquey-sequence," and related "modelling." The task is to produce a paraphrased version of this sentence while preserving its original meaning but using different words and structures, without adding external explanations or summaries.

Current methods for estimating treatment effects in dynamic settings often employ a shrinkage strategy by relying on historical data to regularize current estimates. A primary drawback of these techniques is their failure to account for the specific historical data used, treating it as equally informative. We introduce a Bayesian framework for dynamic treatment strategies that explicitly incorporates historical data while enhancing the pessimistic view of past performance to achieve more reliable effect estimates. Our approach updates historical estimates only when current evidence strongly contradicts initial assumptions, thereby preventing premature reliance on potentially outdated trends. We demonstrate this methodology using a simulation study and apply it to recommend treatments for alcohol use disorder via the Web Quizzes for Harm Reduction platform.

This paper explores the application of homological invariants, specifically derived categories of module categories, in representing dualities found within the broader realm of algebra. It highlights the utility of derived categories of finite modules over finite algebraic structures and derived categories of finite Gelfand-Klimchev modules, alongside derived categories of finite Grothendiech modules defined through homological duality, all within the context of derived dualities. Derived Morita theorems, which establish equivalences between derived categories of modules over different algebras by preserving certain invariants, are also examined. A focus is placed on the connection provided by derived Morita theorems, alongside examples of derived dualities arising from derived Calabi-Yau properties and derived Skew-Calabi-Yau. Further analysis includes discussion on derived Morita theorems, derived Skew-Calabi-Yau properties, and connections to homological invariants, derived Skew-Calabi-Yau properties, and derived Skew-Calabi-Yau properties, all of which are relevant to understanding these concepts. We present an algorithm for explicitly constructing finite quantum state spaces based on $E_8$ lattice models. In this framework, quantum states are represented as Fock space elements formed by tensor products of $E_8$ root vectors, with corresponding measurement operators defined as Weyl group elements. We investigate the resulting state spaces for various symmetries—specifically quotients by $Z_2$, $Z_3$, and $Z_4$, or exact extensions by $Z_4$—and analyze associated observables defined as generators of the braid group $B_3$ and its higher-dimensional extensions. Our results demonstrate that fundamental quantum phenomena, including contextuality and entanglement, persist within these finite state spaces. Notably, we uncover that correlations in these systems surpass the limits of Bell inequalities applicable to both quantum and classical models, exceeding even the maximum real-valued bounds observed in standard quantum mechanics. These findings suggest that essential quantum characteristics rely solely on the underlying complex number structure. This leads to the conjecture that the complexification of $E_7$ might constitute a foundational element of quantum theory, with Fock space elements derived from $E_8$ providing a universal repository for all quantum states.

Multiple-body entanglement is a defining trait of exotic states of condensed matter arising from interactions. In systems featuring flat bands, these interactions can drive symmetry-breaking phenomena even as local effects dominate, since kinetic contributions vanish in such bands we seek to understand how interactions combine with band geometry to foster unique superconductivity. In this work, a model of twisted bilayer graphene is examined to demonstrate that multiple-body bound states can emerge within flat bands exhibiting rich spectral traits. By applying a phenomenological approach to simulate twisted monolayer Bechgaard salts, two-dimensional systems with magic-angle connections, and other topological flat band configurations, it becomes evident that superconducting pairing can exhibit unconventional angular momentum $l > 1$ symmetries. These findings suggest that non-trivial band geometry promotes higher-angular-momentum pairing through enhanced multiple-body correlations.

The well-known Polya's theorem establishes that any real continuous one-dimensional linked system comprises at most two components, with the same conclusion applying to complex ones. This paper demonstrates a finding with a similar spirit for locally compact abelian (LCA) groups: for any linking map from a LCA group to itself, the preimage of any element has an LCA structure whose dimension does not exceed that of the original group's total space. Furthermore, using standard duality principles and a version of the open mapping theorem, this theory yields a general version of Polya's theorem suitable for linked LCA groups.

Presence-absence data, also known as binary data, frequently arise in ecological research. However, standard clustering techniques developed for continuous data often fail when applied to this specific data type. While ecologists traditionally rely on data transformation followed by continuous-data-based clustering, there is a growing interest in methods tailored specifically for binary data. To address this, we evaluated various clustering approaches for binary data, including transformations of binary matrices alongside distance-based, model-based, and tree-based methodologies. Using a simulation framework grounded in realistic continuous data generation but featuring binary row expressions, we assessed these eight distinct methods. Results indicated that models assuming exchangeability across groups produced superior performance. Additionally, incorporating genetic distance derived from an underlying continuous profile into both the transformation and the subsequent model-based clustering processes enhanced accuracy. Finally, we provide accessible R code implementing these recommended binary-specific techniques.

Salient object detection focuses on identifying salient regions within an image to compress them into a binary mask with a hole for the central core. While numerous approaches have been developed for RGB inputs, extending these techniques to RGB-D data remains underexploored. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework unifying various detection strategies for both RGB and RGB-D scenarios. We demonstrate that effective detection can be achieved by synthesizing three core components: a shape prior, a saliency measure, and a depth-aware boundary refiner. By employing a simple yet potent combination of shapes, intrinsic saliency, and the free-space potential function, our method produces state-of-the-art results on SOD benchmark datasets using RGB images. Furthermore, this approach yields highly competitive performance on RGB-D challenges, with the generated masks showing exceptional accuracy when evaluated against ground truth annotations.

This paper details our winning submission for UM-IU@LING at the 6th SemEval shared task on detecting harmful speech in tweets. Our approach combines two BERT models trained on specific datasets to generate feature representations, which are subsequently classified using a support vector machine (SVM). This hybrid method achieved the second-best overall performance among all shared tasks submissions, with an F1 score of 59.99% specifically for the aggressive detection subtask.

Let Q(n) represent the collection of quotients derived from dividing 2's powers (quoticients of symmetrical numbers). This paper demonstrates that every element in Q(n) can be expressed as the product of an element from Q(n) and an element from A(n), where A(n) comprises quotients of antisymmetrical numbers.

Computed Tomography (CT) is a vital medical imaging technique that generates scans using multiple energy levels, or polyenergies, to enhance image quality and accelerate acquisition by allowing higher x-ray doses. However, elevating x-ray throughput often degrades resolution and increases patient radiation exposure. Consequently, reducing the dose while maintaining diagnostic efficacy is a critical challenge. This study introduces a comprehensive, non-convex variational model designed to simultaneously reconstruct images across different materials and denoise CT data from noisy sensors. The proposed framework integrates a data fidelity term accounting for polyenergetic characteristics with three smoothness priors representing cross-sectional slices, polymeric densities, and polymeric energies respectively. Specifically, the smoothness prior for each polymeric density is derived from its corresponding slice representation to achieve accurate material breakdown. CT reconstruction within this scheme relies on the total variation (TV) of each polymeric density's slice. Experimental validation includes simulations and tests on real CT scans of phantoms (both plastic and human), with results indicating superior noise suppression and image clarity compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) is a highly valuable multilingual task with numerous valuable applications. While large datasets like GTR-20 allow for robust model training and performance, low-resource scenarios present a significant challenge due to scarce training data. This study addresses this issue by proposing single-shot compositional data generation, a method designed to create synthetic training data from isolated character images. Comprehensive evaluations across various low-resource languages reveal that our approach, combined with standard data augmentation techniques, surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks in two instances and matches external state-of-the-art methods in the remaining instances.

This work examines first-principles nuclear models with emphasis on including heavy nuclei. We achieve this by incorporating heavy nuclei into large-scale Monte Carlo simulations and conducting ab initio calculations using a chiral two-body interaction, specifically the $V_{low k}$ form. To model three-body forces appropriately, a scaling approximation is applied. The results from these calculations align well with experimental binding energies, demonstrating that binding saturates at a consistent density as the neutron-to-proton ratio varies. Additionally, binding energies for the heaviest nuclei analyzed match experimental data with relative errors below 1%. The study also investigates surface properties through semi-local density expansions, revealing that surface symmetry energy is sensitive to the choice of truncation in the shell model. Finally, surface properties are analyzed using density expansions that are both semi-local and many-body in nature. The surface symmetry energy is found to be sensitive to the choice of two-body and approximate treatment of three-body interactions. This study examines key aspects of topological quantum phenomena using the SSH (Su-Schrieffer-Heeger) model, a1D system. We define and discuss the significance of chiral and quantum numbers in this model. Topological phases are analyzed by measuring end-point states, contrasting them with a trivial phase, and validating results via conductance calculations that align with experimental predictions. Furthermore, we explore various end-point state characteristics, including their robustness against perturbations and spatial decay rates, providing supplementary mathematical derivations. Findings are verified experimentally, and the paper concludes with suggestions for further research.

This study investigates when composition operators induced by continuous self-mappings of strongly pseudoconvex compact domains in C^n are compact on the Bergman space. It derives necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of composition operators associated with maps into C that do not touch the boundary, as well as for those pertaining to maps that remain within the domain. A significant component of the argument involves a generalized version of an interpolation theorem originally due to Carleson. The work also provides characterizations for when induced compositions are compact resulting from mappings onto an analytic disk staying strictly inside an arbitrary convex strong pseudoconvex compact domain in C^2. Finally, by extending previous findings to higher dimensions, it establishes conditions for the compactness of compositions from maps onto an analytic polyhedron in C^n staying strictly inside a strong convex pseudoconvex compact domain.

Using the fact that the dualities of the five-dimensional super Yang-Mills (5D SYM) theory can be derived from its 4-conformal field theory (CFT) via AdS$_6$×S$^5$ holography, we establish that all known dualities in the 5D SYM are likewise traced back to their 4-conformal source. Notably, we identify a set of 5D dualities with no corresponding precedent in the 4-conformal side, suggesting the existence of additional symmetries within that higher-dimensional conformal theory. Furthermore, we propose an extension of the duality web to include 5D magnetic gauge theories, specifically the $SO(5)$ and $Sp(5)$ theories, which engage in interactions with gravity in AdS$_6$ and exhibit interconnections with each other through these underlying 4-conformal symmetries.

Object-oriented programming is widely adopted for developing applications that run on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). Nevertheless, existing GPU memory allocators are primarily engineered for C-style code and fail to address the unique characteristics and performance demands of object-oriented domains. Consequently, critical issues such as fragmented memory and inefficient handling remain unresolved, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocation system designed specifically for object-oriented development on GPUs. This framework integrates several innovative features: a fragmentation-aware strategy for selecting contiguous memory blocks, a load-balancing approach for managing multiple allocators, and a technique leveraging GPU registers to enhance allocation speed. Experimental results indicate that DynsoAR surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions by delivering better fragmentation awareness and faster allocation rates.

We examine the origin of $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry within framework of $SO(10)$ grand unification, which breaks down to the standard model. The model features three generations of standard model fermions, a right-handed neutrino per generation, and two Higgs $SU(2)_L$ doublets. We explore the constraints on $U(1)_X$ charges imposed by gauge anomaly cancellation, showing these are uniquely solved with a right-handed neutrino present. Additionally, we verify that the $SO(10)$ gauge interactions remain intact. Although the specific form of the $U(1)_X$ charge spectrum is not uniquely fixed by this theory, we demonstrate that it can be fully specified by the requirement that $U(1)_X$ must remain unbroken at the $10^{16}$ GeV scale. Under these conditions, the charges are uniquely determined, allowing for a check of the mass spectrum of the resulting standard model.

For detecting pressurized liquid scintillators, a mechanical straw detector features a paper or plastic cylindrical tube coated with photomultiplier sensors. Based on a mechanical analysis of such pressurized conduits, this paper demonstrates that longitudinal tension significantly influences the tube's stability. Consequently, axial detectors like the MWCS, subject to axial compression from the support framework, risk structural failure in the cylindrical walls due to combined pressurized loading and external compression.

Probing the upper bound ensures reliable decision-making, yet calculating it remains a major obstacle for many Bayesian inference tasks. Recently, the credale framework has gained traction for resolving this issue. This approach utilizes an over-relaxation technique that makes the obstacle of determining exact bounds manageable by formally linking it to the width-based verification problem. We observe that this problem can be solved more efficiently than previously thought using modern $\mathsf{CP}$-constraint programming techniques applied to probabilistic circuits. Furthermore, we demonstrate empirically that the credale framework yields superior results for practical decisions compared to the traditional method of sampling-based Monte Carlo. Together, these findings position the credale framework as a viable practical tool for real-world decision-making.

This study investigates the generation of oscillations similar to Bloch oscillations within a two-dimensional Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) superfluid occupying an optical lattice with tilted potential slopes. Oscillations arise due to the acceleration of a wavepacket, prompting an analysis of both low-energy superfluid excitations and lattice vibrations (phonons) through the BKT framework under band-theory conditions. We demonstrate that when a tilted lattice is subjected to acceleration, emergent superfluid oscillations occur, with Amplitude determined by lateral lattice dimensions and potential shape, as opposed to longitudinal lattice spacing. Furthermore, we examine how smooth lattice profiles influence these oscillations and calculate the corresponding wave action.

In a generalized quadrangle $\mathcal{Q}(m,q)$, a subset $\mathcal{C}$ of points constitutes a code with radius $r$ and radius $r$ if every ball of radius $r$ centered at a point outside $\mathcal{C}$ intersects $\mathcal{C}$ in a constant number of elements. When such a code exhibits vertex transitivity, it naturally gives rise to neighbor-transitivity, characterized by uniform intersection sizes between $\mathcal{C}$ and every generalized quadrangle structure within it. This research focuses on classifying these neighbor-transitive codes, which necessitates a detailed examination of the associated association scheme. This scheme arises from a symmetric relation defined on $\mathcal{C}$ where two points relate if they share the same distance to all lines in $\mathcal{Q}(m,q)$. Furthermore, our analysis involves demonstrating the existence of eigenvalue multiplicities sufficient to support the construction of these codes.

We introduce a method to determine how mass is distributed in three dimensions by analyzing its correlation with two-dimensional structures, using this approach to map the mass configuration of the Galactic Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Our results reveal that CMZ structures are most heavily weighted along their long axes, with mass distributions that taper off as distance increases from these filaments. When the spatial orientations of individual filaments are considered, the region's total mass appears more uniform than the highly filament-specific local masses suggest. This three-dimensional mass distribution correlates with CMZ observational characteristics, such as the high frequency of star formation and the prevalence of diffuse gas.

We introduce a non-linear, high-fluence X-ray absorption model grounded in a system of rate equations that govern the dynamics of electronic states. This approach utilizes rate constants derived from Fermi's Golden Rule and population dynamics to simulate absorption events, subsequent autoionization, and radiative decay. By employing a system of coupled, non-linear differential equations, the model accurately reproduces experimental features across various core electron shells, including radiative and non-radiative decay processes, as well as autoionization and population dynamics states. Specifically, the model captures a radiative decay state involving the 1s state in oxygen that was previously unaccounted for in standard linear approximations. Furthermore, we examine radiative decay pathways for 2s and 2p states in neon, providing a theoretical basis for corresponding experimental spectra. These results offer insights into how high-fluence X-ray spectra evolve and enable more precise modeling of radiative states in plasma environments.

This study introduces an energy-efficient and temperature-resilient sensor featuring a broad operating voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V, a resolution of 0.24°C, and high accuracy with a maximum combined error of ±1.4°C. The sensor achieves these specifications through a broad-spectrum voltage design utilizing a 1.2V reference source, a band-aid approach to offset non-idealities, and a calibration strategy to minimize temperature-dependent errors. The resulting 0.24°C resolution is derived from the sensor's ability to distinguish minute variations in the environment, while the ±1.4°C accuracy ensures reliable performance across diverse conditions. The sensor's energy efficiency is further highlighted by its low power consumption, averaging approximately 10μA during active conversion and approximately 1μA in standby mode. The total energy per conversion is approximately 10pJ, with a maximum temperature coefficient of approximately 0.1%/°C. The sensor's performance is further enhanced by its ability to operate across a wide range of environmental conditions, including temperatures ranging from -40°C to +85°C and relative humidity levels from 0% to 95%. The sensor's design is further refined by its use of advanced semiconductor processes, which enable its compact size and low cost. The sensor's performance is further validated by its use in various applications, including industrial process monitoring, environmental tracking, and consumer electronics. The sensor's

We introduce a novel method to generate polarization entanglement between two photons, guided by the "quantum scissors" framework, by utilizing spatial modes with diverse spatial diversity factors. This approach eliminates the need for spatial entanglement or specific operations like polarization phase matching typically required in standard protocols. We outline an experimental setup to produce the entangled pair and demonstrate, via simulation of this experiment, that our method is highly robust against defects such as incomplete entanglement in the input state, low conversion efficiency, and low contrast in spatial modes.

We introduce the concept of virtual Euclidean spanners, which comprises a pair consisting of virtual points and their full spanner. The virtual points are defined through their virtual distances, measured as the shortest path lengths across a virtual metric that does not necessarily adhere to geometric constraints, even if the original set of points is embedded in Euclidean space. Our primary finding demonstrates that for any configuration of $n$ virtual points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, one can construct a $\alpha$-shortest path spanner containing at most $\min\{n, \alpha n^{1+d/2}\}$ nodes. Our work also addresses the converse problem: for a given $\alpha$, what structural Euclidean properties must $n$ virtual points possess to force any $\alpha$-shortest path spanner to have a specific size? This line of inquiry yields a characterization for arrangements of vertical and horizontal line segments in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where the number of segments is $n$. Specifically, the vertex count of the minimum-size $\alpha$-shortest path spanner scales as $\Omega(\alpha^{-2})$ for certain configurations, whereas it remains $O(\alpha^{-1})$ for others.

Feature extraction methods are widely utilized to categorize devices within IoT frameworks. While these methods enhance data compression and energy efficiency at the device level, current research largely overlooks the cost associated with signal processing on the user's end. This paper introduces an energy-aware device classification framework designed to address this gap. It proposes three specific metrics to evaluate the operational costs of existing IoT classification methods from a user perspective: first, the raw energy cost of receiving raw signals; second, the energy cost for a user to replicate the device's classification processing; and third, the cost for users to estimate specific features used in classification. Finally, the framework evaluates performance using a dataset derived from Raspberry Pi devices and discusses how a centralized server can be employed to further minimize total user costs.

This study extends previous research by S. A. Gr\"{a}tzel and the present author, focusing on G\"{o}del modal logics (G\"{o}del Creissman algebras), and introduces new examples of G\"{o}dol Crelman algebras. Additionally, the paper establishes frame representation theorems for various G\"{e}sssel modal logics and examines the properties of their corresponding frames. Many of these contributions also apply broadly within the scope of these findings.

We introduce a method for performing real-time word alignment during both speech recognition and recognition, achieving this by integrating external bilingual knowledge sources. Our approach achieves significant reductions in computational complexity from O(N*M) down to O(N*K), where N and M represent the lengths of the target bilingual sequences, and K is a fixed small constant. This optimization is made possible by mapping words to a shared reference language rather than aligning the two source languages directly. Evaluation results on the TTS 2017 task demonstrate that our system reduces end-error rates by 17.0% on a major part of the problem and achieves at least another 17.0% on the other part; similarly, our word-per-word ETL task system delivered an ETL improvement of 17.0% on a subset and saw an additional 17.0% gain on the other subset.

This work introduces a novel algorithm designed to generate Nash equilibria in finite games, leveraging a distorted form of the Brueckner resolver operated within the simplex. For the modified parameter values, the author demonstrates that the method converges linearly to a Nash equilibrium using results derived from the application of a monotone, distorted distance function on the simpleton. Furthermore, it is shown that the Brueckner method represents a specific case of this proposed approach when the relevant parameters revert to their standard settings.

This work provides the first cosmological simulations incorporating Dark Energy in the form of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) with masses around $10^{17}$ g. Such massive PBHs, formed in the early universe, are a potential candidate for Dark Energy, capable of undergoing rapid evaporation in the current epoch to produce detectable gamma-ray signatures. We employ the particle-based PBH formation model from PopSyCLE, which links PBH abundance to features in the primordial power spectrum, and extend this into the later universe by adding a custom module to simulate BHB evaporation via the DECAY code. Our results indicate that, for a universe-dominated by Dark Energy, the subsequent expansion history remains largely unchanged compared to a matter- or Lambda-dominated cosmos, a fact supported by our finding that standard cosmological observables are insensitive to these evaporating PBHs. While this support suggests current observational constraints on early-Universe physics—specifically the restriction on PBH formation derived from the primordial spectrum—are robust, we note that future investigations should explore alternative, non-observational consequences of such an scenario more thoroughly.

This study examines static random fields defined on a sphere that adhere to specific first- or second-order differential equations involving the spherical Laplacian. By deriving recurrence relations for their spectral densities and cross-spectral coefficients, the field's one-step predictability is quantified. Several canonical examples—including spherical harmonics, zonal harmonics, Karhunen–Loève expansions, Markov random fields, and Spherical Harmonic Processes—are analyzed to apply these results. Notably, for these standard cases, the required coefficients are either explicitly known or effectively computable.

We introduce a method for quantum imaging that functions entirely independent of standard detection requirements, utilizing only a single pixel. This technique operates on the principle where light particles are physically prevented from entering the device under specific conditions defined by separate spatial and temporal parameters. This quantum interference occurs within an engine-like arrangement comprising two engine holes leading to that detector. By varying the spatial selection between the holes or the timing of particle introduction, unique quantum signatures are produced. Notably, no quantum signals or entangled pairs at the output serve as these patterns allow for quantum state reconstruction and the differentiation between unknown wavefunctions. Furthermore, this methodology enables quantum imaging and sensing techniques that surpass traditional classical limits. The complex flow behavior of highly viscous, disordered liquids, such as colloidal suspensions and granular pastes, is significantly shaped by friction. This study examines the relationship between friction and flow dynamics in quasi-two-dimensional foams, revealing a strong correlation between local flow velocity and the thermodynamic state of the foam. By employing an original technique to measure local yield stress, we identified that this metric strongly correlates with the local yield stress of the system. Our findings indicate that the coexistence of high yield stress and high viscosity results in a characteristic "textured" structure. Consequently, we propose a simple model that successfully reproduces the experimentally observed non-local effects, specifically the emergence of vortex-like structures within the flow field.

The identification of skin cancer is critical for cancer management, and recent advances in deep learning offer a promising path for automating this process. This paper proposes a pipeline to identify skin carcinomas, utilizing the open dataset ISIC-2018. The method begins with a multi-class classification task using a ResNet neural network on training patches. To ensure robustness, we incorporate an outlier detection technique that flags anomalies in the test set, enabling a re-evaluation of classified results. The proposed approach achieved a accuracy of 89.1%, surpassing previous submissions to the CHICC-2020 challenge, which focused on the same classification task.

We have measured the non-linear optical response of solid sodium, an almost-free electron metal, to continuous-wave laser radiation. By examining the response both with and without DC fields, we determined that electronic quasi-particles possess lifetimes ranging from 10 to 100 femtoseconds. These findings imply a relaxation time for momentum significantly longer than what is predicted by standard nearly-free electron metal theory.

This paper introduces a novel technique designed to tackle challenges related to phase space volume transformation. It defines the concept of the "generalized ensemble," composed of subsystems traversing specific paths in phase space that conform to a prescribed Hamiltonian framework. These subsystems are interconnected such that every point within the overarching phase space receives equal visitation frequency by the ensemble as a whole. By constructing these independent subsystems along a specified trajectory, a flow is established, enabling the calculation of the Jacobian required for phase space volume transformation tasks. The discussion elucidates this definition, explores its fundamental attributes, and utilizes this framework to introduce a new generalized Jacobian derived from flow analysis. It also presents an original approach to implementing global algorithms based on the "Hamiltonian path," originally developed for sampling the Microcanonical Ensemble. Furthermore, it introduces the "Hamiltonian Jacobian" specifically for sampling regions defined by a constrained Hamiltonian flow, utilizing this tool to design advanced sampling strategies.

Self-distillation has emerged as a key method for enhancing deep learning model accuracy. In the field of computer vision, property-aware self-distillation (GASDI) specifically targets improving convolutional neural networks by employing distillation objectives that refine intermediate layer representations. This study investigates the application of such self-distillation techniques to Vision Transformers, the most prevalent architecture in self-guided computer vision. We identify specific shortcomings when adapting property-aware self-distillation directly to Vision Self-Diagnosis. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Self-Bo, a simplified yet highly effective distortion technique tailored for Vision Transformers, which also enables property-conscious self-distillation. Experiments across various vision tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms the leading property-sensitive transformer approach, achieving gains in accuracy ranging from 0.7% to 2.7%.

We investigate an ideal dissipative fluid incorporating a negative bulk viscosity coefficient ($\xi$), interpreting it as composites of dark matter and dark matter that interact through the dissipation process. By analyzing a cosmological model featuring source terms in the continuity equation, we demonstrate that this dissipation mechanism naturally emulates combined dark fluid behavior. Specifically, our results align with observational data indicating a non-conserved energy framework for such fluids. Our analysis reveals that this dissipation-driven, effective combined dark fluid exhibits two distinct characteristics: first, its equation of state transitions smoothly from that of a radiation-dominated era to one resembling dark matter; second, it remains strictly below the critical value of $w=-1/3$, thereby preencing any cosmological repulsive force.

We utilize the method of transport-derived partial differential equations to provide a direct demonstration of well-posedness failure for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations in critical (and lower) Sobolev spaces. This approach extends the technique originally employed by *Kahane* (1969) for the Navier-Stokes equations and the method introduced by *Kist, Raudenbush, and Schickinger* (2021) which was applied to the Prandtl equations. The core mechanism relies on constructing specific monomial functions that satisfy both the given initial value condition and the equation itself, thereby proving the stated result.

Although recent advancements in image generation models have produced remarkable results, researchers are increasingly seeking more precise image synthesis and editing capabilities. This study introduces Steady Creator (DCT-50), a framework designed to control image editing within the latent space of the image diffusion model. By leveraging a "Steady Point" within latent space that maintains structural consistency across conditions, our method enables the directed alteration of specific attributes, such as changing the hue in an image through "staying points." This approach allows control over properties like hair color without unintentionally modifying other structural elements. You can access our pre-trained DCT-50 model at: https://github.com/yzhao062/steady_creator.

Steganography aims to transmit covert messages within innocuous covers without revealing the presence of the hidden data. Recent advances in deep learning, while enhancing visual quality in standard steganographic methods, often degrade it further when employing irreversible techniques. This study introduces a novel irreversible approach that leverages Bayesian neural networks to hide information within color images while preserving visual fidelity. The method utilizes a generative Bayesian model that integrates three components: an encoder for extracting and hiding bits, a posterior calculator for intermediate processing, and a prior-based prior network ensuring high-quality reconstruction. Notably, this architecture allows for dynamic adjustment of both concealment capacity and output fidelity. Extensive experiments conducted on the StebMCo dataset demonstrate that the proposed technique surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods regarding bit per value (BPR) performance while maintaining superior image fidelity scores.

This study investigates a scenario where the missing energy in $J/\psi\to (\gamma + ){\rm invisible}$ decays is attributed to a massive sterile neutrino, specifically addressing the question of its mass scale. We demonstrate that the missing mass spectrum in the decaying state is distributed across a continuous range rather than being confined to a single, fixed mass. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of dark matter production on cosmological scales, specifically addressing neutrino oscillation parameters and constraints on neutrino masses. We also examine how the dark energy sector interacts with the universe's accelerated expansion. Finally, we outline the experimental signatures that could reveal this neutrino state and illustrate its potential implications within the frameworks of effective field theories for both neutrino physics and dark energy.

High-resolution observations of magnetic bright spots (spots) on the solar surface reveal that their brightness profiles are consistently well-modeled by a combination of a Gaussian distribution and a power-law. While the specific shape of these brightness profiles is primarily dictated by the physical characteristics of magnetic spots, it is influenced by numerous factors, notably leading to broadened profiles that are often deemed impractical for precise measurements of spot size. However, this study demonstrates that the superposition of a Gaussian component and a power-law is a generic characteristic of solar magnetic spot brightness. We propose an alternative interpretation: this profile does not necessarily reflect the intrinsic physical structure of a single spot but rather represents the statistical convergence of diverse individual spot populations. Supporting this view, observations indicate that bright spots within one supergranule exhibit power-law-like fluctuations in intensity, whereas they follow Gaussian statistics when viewed across the entire solar disk. Consequently, brightness profiles across the sun likely mask the distinct physical properties of individual spots, thereby impeding accurate measurement. We further suggest that accounting for the variability in the power-law index of local intensity fluctuations can effectively correct for obscuring effects, enabling more precise and reliable sizing of magnetic spots.

Current dynamic identification research primarily focuses on maximizing the use of available information, yet a limitation remains: not all models capture how humans actually perceive identities. This study introduces a human-centric approach by collecting "minimal clips"—short video segments containing sufficient identity details—through experiments where participants watched clips and distinguished between familiar and unknown faces using a 2AFC task. The data revealed that people require significantly shorter videos to recognize identity information than existing recognition algorithms. To address this, the authors introduce a new loss function grounded in information theory, aiming to represent only essential identity features for human dynamic recognition and test its efficacy within a feature extraction network. Results indicate that this proposed method substantially improves identity matching performance when working with very short duration footage.

We introduce an axion-like shadow matter model featuring monopole-couplings on the milli-scale that could explain the persistence of galactic magnetic fields. In this framework, a global symmetry breaks spontaneously, yielding a composite particle as the corresponding axion-like matter. This matter is produced through the interaction of monopoles with the axion-like shadow. This model is characterized by two parameters: the monopole-fidelity-coupling-strength ($g_m$) and the axion-like-shadow-mass ($m_a$). We analyze the parameter space using two constraints: (1) existing limits on oscillations of the axion-like shadow from laboratory experiments, and (2) a new constraint derived from galaxy formation regarding the suppression of cold dark matter power spectrum at small scales. We find that if $m_a$ falls below approximately 100 keV, $g_m$ must be less than $10^{-13}$. This upper limit on $g_m$ suggests that early universe magnetic fields would dissipate within a Hubble time, conflicting with the observed galactic magnetic fields. We further examine how this new shadow matter influences recombination-era physics and the resulting Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies.

Accurately projecting future spatiotemporal climate patterns is vital for planning societal responses to global warming. Transformer architectures have recently shown strong capabilities in modeling long-range dependencies for such data. However, existing approaches often rely on 2D or 3D convolutional layers that degrade performance on extensive sequences and struggle with efficient cross-attention mechanisms across entire sequences. To address these limitations, this study introduces ST-TSXLW, a new Transformer model designed for predicting extended sequences in climate data. This architecture employs two core components: 2D shifted window-based multi-head attention to handle large spatiotemporal inputs efficiently, and a novel 1D temporal attention mechanism to capture cross-temporal dependencies effectively. Empirical evaluations using three real-world datasets demonstrate that ST-TSXLW significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in forecasting long-duration climate sequences.

We examine scalar dark matter models featuring two complex Higgs doublets, which inherently possess ten real degrees of freedom, subject to an $S_3$ symmetry that reduces this count by five to yield five physical states. This setup allows the dark matter candidate to interact with both inert and active components of the scalar sector. We analyze the model's phenomenology in the regime where vacuum expectation values are small, focusing on tree-level phenomenology alongside one- and two-loop corrections to the dark matter relic density. Specifically, we investigate the impact of loop-induced couplings on the scalar dark matter annihilation cross-section, incorporating electroweak corrections as well as self-interaction and Y-type couplings within specific limits. Our results demonstrate that while self-couplings have limited significance, contributions from $Y$-type couplings play a pivotal role in determining the relic density. Furthermore, we explore LHC phenomenology by assessing the reach of Run 2 and future Run 3 experiments in detecting these signatures.

In this study, we formulate a mathematical model to simulate ion transport within neurons, accounting for ion channel regulation and congestion effects. Our objective function aims to stabilize neuronal ion levels by minimizing deviations from target concentrations, subject to PDEs representing ions' congested dynamics governed by the Navier-Stege equations with Squire flow and Fick's second law of diffusion. To address this PDE-constrained optimization challenge, we derive the objective function's gradient using an adjoint state technique and implement our approach using the IPOPS solver available in the CasADi framework. Validation of the proposed model and optimization framework is performed using two standard neuronal morphologies: the simplified ball-and-stick structure and detailed experimental data for a CA3 hippocampal pyramidal neuron.

This paper introduces an unsupervised approach to identify network motifs within the finance network network. By detecting these local structures, we can infer the underlying mechanisms governing how the network evolves. Using an real-world dataset of historical stock transactions as a case study, we identified and analyzed several distinct motifs. Our findings reveal that these patterns align with theoretical models based on wealth distribution dynamics, specifically those involving social learning and status-driven interactions, indicating that these motivation-driven behaviors drive the network's evolution.

We have performed 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations to examine the star's emissions as it is consumed by a supermassive black hole, a process that can mimic the signatures of the tidal disruption event (TDE) where a star is devoured. The scenario involves a star reaching the point of direct disruption at the black hole's horizon, an event that results in the immediate accretion of the star's material. The event horizon acts as an anchor for the magnetic field lines, which, combined with the infalling material, generate strong magnetic fields within the black hole's accretion flow. These fields drive powerful jets, which are responsible for the majority of the radiated energy. The simulations reveal that the jets are highly collimated and originate from the innermost regions of the system, while the accretion disk forms further out. The event horizon's role in twisting magnetic field lines is the mechanism that launches and shapes these energetic jets.

This paper examines Baryonic form factors in the context of three-body $\tau$ decays, including the $\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, and $N$ strangeness-changing ($\Delta S=1$) and strangeness-conserving ($\Delta S=0$) strangeness-neutral categories. We employ a series expansion of form factors in terms of the timelike momentum transfer squared ($q^2$), leveraging the analyticity properties of these structures as dictated by dispersion relations. Our analysis incorporates constraints derived from unitarity, which limit the form factors based on their hadronic spectrum and coupling constants. Specifically, we integrate lattice Qtd determinations of form factors at low $q^2$ values and utilize theoretical estimates for the spectral function spectral density at higher $q^2$. By applying these inputs, we predict the form factors for every relevant channel and compare our results against available experimental data.

This paper introduces a family of Tversky metrics parameterized by the sum of two distances, denoted as $d_{TW}(D_1,D_2|\alpha)$ for $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$. We demonstrate that this framework encompasses the standard Tversky distance (corresponding to $\alpha=1$) as a specific subset and that, particularly for $\alpha > 1$, it surpasses previous work restricting parameters to natural numbers. We position this parametric form within the study of generalized set distances, specifically as a generalized Jaccard distance, and establish its relationship to and distinctness from the normalized information distance (NID). We provide a mathematical proof that, for any pair of non-empty sets, the Tversky distance is strictly smaller than the NID.

Deblurring deformed images containing humans or scenes is a difficult task due to ambiguous reconstruction possibilities. To address this, we introduce a new approach for deblurring distorted images of people or settings by utilizing a pseudo-blur conditional generative adversarial network (pCGAN). Our method creates deblurred content that is conditionally aligned with the underlying 3D structure of the original image. This alignment helps the network generate a more singular, structurally coherent latent representation, effectively resolving ambiguity. Furthermore, we propose two new deblur strategies targeting different structural features: the first aligns with the image's semantic layout using a sparse point cloud derived from a depth-sparse model, while the second aligns with the dense 3D geometry using points extracted from the optical flow of the deblurred result. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed deblurring framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce a framework-driven approach for designing and simulating moles (molecular computing systems) so that their operational output converges on the behavior of specific target neurons. To validate this method, we focused on the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire neuron, demonstrating that a moles design constructed from just a few hundred enzymes can accurately emulate its axon spiking dynamics. Furthermore, we found that this valid moles system can internalize external stimulus sequences and extract core features of the generated output signals. The success of this study highlights the potential of framework-based architecture design for creating moles that not only replicate desired physiological reactions but also execute specialized computational tasks.

Let $(A,\le_A)$ represent a partially ordered set (poset), where the collection of its chains forms an equivalence relation denoted as $\mathcal{C}(A)$. This generates the quotient structure, known as the chain quotient $(A/\!\!\mathcal{C}(A), \le_{\mathcal{C}(A)})$. We define a binary relation $\preceq$ on the quotient such that two elements are related if their representatives in $A$ satisfy the original order; this induces a partial order on $(A/\!\!\mathcal{C}(A)) \times (A/\!\!\mathcal{C}(A))$. By constructing the chain quotient of this newly ordered space, we obtain a directed graph whose connected components yield a directed set, formally another quotient of $(A/\!\!\mathcal{C}(A)) \times (A/\!\!\mathcal{C}(A))$. Our analysis reveals that this resulting structure is always equivalent as a directed set to the original chain quotient $(A/\!\!\mathcal{C}(A))$. Applying these observations to linear structures leads to the conclusion that the chain quotient of the linear order is itself a linear order. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of ultrapowers constructed from these chain quotients.

Although deep learning models have transformed natural language processing, their susceptibility to data skew makes them ill-suited for many production environments. Current evaluation practices, which rely on static, large-scale benchmarks, fail to capture such data variability. This study introduces a rigorous framework for producing provably accurate data profiles that are tailored to specific datasets and demonstrates its application in a novel method for quantifying the bias of these skewed productions. Evaluated across three distinct tasks—machine translation, semantic role labeling, and question answering—the proposed bias metric identifies production issues previously overlooked by standard metrics like BLEU or average precision.

We introduce a new generation method for highly entangled spin states within an interferometer involving two spinor components, enabling the creation of a variety of states through simple interference patterns. These quantum states exhibit novel entanglement characteristics that allow the spin Squeezing Parameter to surpass the standard -3 limit. A full analysis of experimental feasibility is provided, including an evaluation of how practical constraints impact performance. Additionally, we discuss diverse applications of these states, ranging from precision measurements to error correction and the implementation of specific quantum algorithms.
